docs.title: Beginner Projects
docs.text:
These examples outline how to turn a LiDAR use case into an application. Each starts with a goal, a sensor-to-application data path, and practical steps for prototyping and validation. Level 1 projects introduce guided sensor applications, Level 2 adds 3D evaluation, point-cloud tools, native ROS 2 SLAM, or an IMU-controlled game, and Level 3 combines SDK wrappers, asynchronous field status, runtime field selection, and image visualization.

Beginner Projects: level, example, compatible device family, and goal. Model names in parentheses identify the model used in the example.

Level Example Compatible device family Goal 1 Building Security LRS4000, picoScan family Monitor an area (e.g. a room floor) very precisely. 1 Bulk Scan LRS4000, picoScan family Measure the material height on a conveyor belt as a starting point for bulk-material profiles. 2 3D Height Measurement multiScan100 family Measure body height with a multiScan100 using perpendicular distance above a floor reference. 2 House in 3D LRS4000, picoScan family (picoScan150) Record picoScan 3D point clouds around a house and inspect the exported PCD files. 2 Reversing Assistant picoScan family (picoScan150) Detect the closest obstacle behind a vehicle and flash the warning LEDs faster as it gets closer. 2 Native ROS 2 SLAM picoScan family (picoScan150) Build a map and localize a vehicle within it using native ROS 2 and SLAM Toolbox. 2 picoScan150 Jump & Run picoScan family (picoScan150) Use picoScan IMU data, a generated Kaitai Python parser, and a browser game to turn sensor movement into player movement. 2 Smart Shelf picoScan family (picoScan150) Detect which shelf compartment a pen reaches into using picoScan perpendicular distance and WebSocket events in a browser. 3 ROS 2 Reversing Assistant with an Ambient-Light Image multiScan200 family (multiScan270) Wrap multiScan270 SDK data for ROS 2 over Zenoh, display an ambient image, receive field events, and switch near/wide groups.

docs.title: Building Security Example
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 picoScan100

Security access gates form a transition between secure and non-secure areas of an airport. An object-detection check can help identify items left in the gate area before access is granted.

Example security-door installation. The red overlay illustrates the detection area; the inset shows the LiDAR sensor mounting position.

A compact 2D LiDAR sensor can monitor a configured detection zone and report objects that interrupt the scan or differ from a taught reference contour. This can support a security workflow concerned with prohibited items, such as weapons, but LiDAR object detection alone does not identify an object's type or determine whether it is prohibited. Validate detection coverage and performance for the installation and combine it with the required security checks.

docs.title: Suggested Data Path
docs.text:
Configure the detection zone with teach-in:

  1. In SOPASair, open the Object Detection application and select Teach-in in the field configuration.
  2. Set the distances in front of and behind the object and the minimum teach-in time, then click Start.
  3. Keep the gate area empty and stable, stop the teach-in, and save the field evaluation configuration.
  4. Check the result: with the gate area empty, the field is free; place a test object in it and confirm that the field is infringed.

docs.title: Example Solution
docs.text:
The following video demonstrates teach-in for a building-security example.

Teach-in demonstration for the building-security example.

docs.title: Bulk Scan
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 picoScan100

This project measures the height of woodchips or other bulk material on a conveyor belt. Mounted above the belt, the sensor scans the material surface and reports its distance to the empty belt. It is a height measurement, not a calibrated volume measurement; a volume estimate needs your own processing.

Example woodchip conveyor installation. The highlighted scan area covers the material profile across the belt.

Use Perpendicular Distance Measurement as a starting point for measuring material height:

  1. In SOPASair, open Application > Perpendicular distance measurement and add an evaluation group.
  2. Draw the zone across the belt and set the reference line to the empty belt surface.
  3. Save the configuration and read the minimum and maximum distances from the result list or GET /api/perpendicularDistanceResult.
  4. Check the result: with an empty belt, no distance is reported; with a test object of known height on the belt, the maximum distance matches that height.

To estimate volume throughput, your application can calculate the cross-sectional area from the scan profile and multiply it by the belt speed.

Perpendicular-distance measurement demonstration for the woodchip example.

docs.title: 3D Height Measurement
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100

A multiScan100 can measure the body height of a person in a defined area. The sensor scans the area in 3D, while perpendicular-distance evaluation measures the detected points relative to the floor. The maximum distance inside the evaluation field represents the person's height.

A 3D LiDAR measures people as they pass through a defined detection area.

docs.title: Suggested Data Path
docs.text:
1. Mount the multiScan100 so its field of view covers the measuring area and the top of the person's head remains within the scan range.
  2. Create an evaluation group in Application > Perpendicular distance measurement and draw a field around the measuring area.
  3. Use the floor as the reference plane. Keep walls, door frames, and other fixed objects outside the field so they cannot become the maximum value.
  4. Configure the object-detection settings for stable measurements.
  5. Read the minimum and maximum perpendicular distances from the evaluation result. Use the maximum distance as the measured body height.

For configuration and result-access details, see Perpendicular Distance Measurement.

docs.title: Example Solution
docs.text:
The following screenshot shows the evaluation in SOPASair. The 3D field covers the person above the floor, and the result list reports the minimum and maximum distances for the evaluation.

Height-measurement example using perpendicular distance. The maximum distance of 1766 mm represents the measured body height.

Validate the setup with people of known height and verify that the reported maximum remains stable as a person moves through the measuring area.

docs.title: House in 3D
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 picoScan100

This example shows how to use a picoScan150 3D scan recording as a starting point for documenting a building. The sensor combines its 2D scan profiles with rotation information from its internal IMU or an external encoder and exports the result as a .pcd point-cloud file.

docs.title: Suggested Data Path
docs.text:
The on-device scan merger records one point cloud at a time.

Mount and orient the sensor so its scan plane sweeps the area of interest as it rotates. Configure an IMU or encoder rotation source and the sensor offset in Application → 3D scan recording; see 3D Scan Recording. Clear the previous recording, capture the sweep, stop recording, and wait for saving to finish. Download /cloud.pcd before starting the next capture; the device keeps only the most recent point cloud.

docs.title: Example Solution
docs.text:
The video demonstrates capturing the house as a 3D point cloud with picoScan150:

picoScan150 3D scan recording of the house in SOPASair.

Open each .pcd capture in CloudCompare to inspect coverage, identify missing areas, and compare the separate viewpoints.

docs.title: picoScan150 Jump & Run
docs.text:
Compatible with: picoScan100

Build picoScan150 Jump & Run and use the built-in IMU of a picoScan as a game controller. Move the sensor left or right and the player runs with it; a quick upward hop makes it jump. Points grow with time, and the game gets faster every 15 seconds. No scan data is used.

picoScan150 Jump & Run: moving the sensor steers the player.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
• How to enable the IMU stream over REST and receive it as Compact type 2 over UDP.
  • How to check the CRC32 and decode the telegrams with a generated Kaitai parser.
  • How to turn acceleration into robust movement events.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• A picoScan with IMU streaming, for example picoScan150, on the same network as your computer (Getting Started).
  • Python, a browser, the Kaitai Struct compiler and runtime, and sick_scan_rest_client.
  • Hold the sensor firmly with slack in the cables. Short moves of 10 to 20 cm are enough.
  • Set the environment variable SICK_PASSWORD to the Service password. The default passwords are documented in the operating instructions of your device. Do not pass them on, and change them during commissioning.

docs.title: Data Path
docs.text:
picoScan IMU → UDP → CRC32 check → Kaitai Python parser → motion controller → local web server → browser game

Python receives the UDP datagrams and serves the Canvas game on 127.0.0.1. Generate the parser from the official Compact frame and type-2 IMU definitions. The parser does not verify the checksum; check the CRC32 first (Reception and Validation).

docs.title: Configure IMU Output
docs.text:
The game sets up the stream through the REST interface at start and disables it on exit:

import os

from sick_scan_rest_client.client import RESTClient

client = RESTClient("192.168.0.1")  # sensor IP address
client.setUserLevel("Service", os.environ["SICK_PASSWORD"])
client.writeVariable("ImuDataEthSettings",
                     {"Protocol": 1, "IPAddress": [192, 168, 0, 100], "Port": 7503})
client.writeVariable("ImuDataEnable", True)

Send the IMU stream by UDP (Protocol 1) to the computer at 192.168.0.100, port 7503. The change is RAM-only.

Keep both IP addresses and the port configurable. If the sensor streams but nothing arrives, the computer's firewall is the usual cause; allow the port or pick one that is permitted.

docs.title: How Movement Works
docs.text:
The game uses gravity-corrected acceleration, not tilt. To calibrate, hold the sensor still, then push it right once.

↑ Quick hop to jump ← Move left

Move the sensor sideways to steer; lift it for a quick hop to jump.

Move right →

Game controls.

Control Response Move sensor left or right Player runs left or right. Quick upward hop One jump. Start, Pause, Stop Run, freeze, or end the game. Calibrate Hold still, then push right once. Settings Sensor IP, computer IP, port, sensitivity. Arrow keys and Space Play without a sensor.

Jump over blocks, dodge falling rocks from level 2, and collect coins. You score 10 points per second and 50 per coin. The game pauses if IMU data stops for 500 ms.

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
• Without a sensor, play with the keyboard; the high score survives a restart.
  • With the sensor, the status shows about 100 valid packets per second.
  • Holding still or tilting slowly does not move the player; a short move right does, then stops.
  • A quick hop gives exactly one jump; a sideways push gives none.
  • Quitting the program switches the IMU stream off.

docs.title: Project Prompt
docs.text:
Paste this prompt into your coding assistant in a new workspace. It asks for the receiver, the game, tests, and a Windows executable.

Expand to view the complete project prompt 
Build a beginner-friendly level-two project called "picoScan150 Jump & Run":
a SICK picoScan150 IMU is the game controller for a basic browser
jump-and-run game. The player moves left and
right when I move the sensor left and right (use the measured acceleration,
not tilt), and jumps when I lift the sensor with a quick upward hop.
Deliver working files, not a plan. Work in a new folder outside the
developer guide. Use Python 3.12, the Kaitai Struct Python runtime, requests,
sick_scan_rest_client (https://github.com/SICKAG/sick_scan_rest_client) and
plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Canvas. Use only the Python standard
library for the web server. No ROS, SICK SDK, scan data, point clouds,
frontend framework or external game assets. Keep the code easy to follow.
Draw the player as a small picoScan: grey housing with a blue SICK badge,
black optics dome with a moving red scan point, short legs, and a faint scan
fan in the running direction.

1. Configuration
Read config.json next to the program (create it with defaults on first start)
and allow command-line overrides: sensor IP (default 192.168.0.1), PC IP on
the sensor network (default 192.168.0.100), UDP port (default 7503), local
HTTP port (default 8765), --no-configure and --no-browser. Validate IPv4
addresses and ports. Offer the same settings in a Settings dialog in the game,
list the PC's local IPv4 addresses as suggestions, save changes back to
config.json and reconnect without restarting the program.

2. Sensor setup with REST
At start, in a background thread, use sick_scan_rest_client: RESTClient(ip),
setUserLevel("Service", password from config), then writeVariable
"ImuDataEthSettings" = {"Protocol": 1, "IPAddress": [PC IP octets],
"Port": udp port} and "ImuDataEnable" = true. Check reachability with a short
TCP connect to port 80 first, because the client sets no timeouts. Bypass any
system HTTP proxy for the sensor IP. writeVariable returns (ok, data);
check ok. Both variables need the Service level. Use UDP: TCP output
(Protocol 2) was refused in tests, and polling the IMU over REST only
updates at about 4 Hz, which is too slow for a game. These are RAM-only
changes; do not call WriteEeprom. Show the result in the UI. On exit set
ImuDataEnable = false. On Windows, atexit does not run when the console
window is closed, so also register a console control handler
(SetConsoleCtrlHandler) for close and Ctrl+Break. Keep scan settings
untouched.

3. Receive and decode with the real Kaitai parser
Generate Python from SICKAG/KaitaiStructDescriptions (public branch),
formats/compact_frame.ksy with all imported formats, using
kaitai-struct-compiler -t python --outdir <dir> formats/*.ksy. Keep the
generated modules unmodified and record the command. They import each other
as top-level modules, so add their folder to sys.path, and use the
kaitaistruct runtime 0.11 or newer. Do not replace Kaitai
with a hand-written struct parser. Bind a UDP socket to the PC IP and port,
accept datagrams only from the sensor IP, check the start bytes 02 02 02 02,
verify CRC32 (zlib.crc32 over all bytes except the trailing 4-byte
little-endian checksum), then parse with CompactFrame and accept only
telegram_type == 2. Count good and rejected frames, compute the packet rate
(about 100 Hz on picoScan150) and keep the receiver alive on bad packets.
Report bind errors clearly (for example, the PC IP is not on this computer).
Record a few hundred real frames to a file for the tests.

4. Turn acceleration into controls
Rotate the acceleration into the world frame with the orientation quaternion
(w, x, y, z) and subtract a gravity/bias vector, so tilting the sensor does
not look like sideways motion. On picoScan150 the quaternion is
gravity-referenced: R(q) * acc is about (0, 0, 9.8) at rest. Without the
rotation, a 20 degree tilt leaks about 3.4 m/s^2 into the sideways axis and
the velocity drifts. Yaw has no magnetometer reference and can drift slowly,
so offer recalibration. Estimate that vector automatically from the
first 1.5 s, and track it slowly while the sensor is quiet.
Calibrate button: 1.5 s still (reject if the per-axis standard deviation is
above 0.35 m/s^2), then "move the sensor quickly to the RIGHT once": the
horizontal direction of the strongest push sample (above 2 m/s^2) becomes
the right axis. Without calibration, use the sensor y axis projected into
the horizontal plane. Add an invert option.
Sideways input: dead zone 0.35 m/s^2, then integrate into a velocity with a
leak (time constant 0.8 s while moving, 0.12 s after 0.15 s of quiet), so it
returns to zero when the sensor stops. The leak recovers only about half
of the real movement, so scale the velocity in the game (about 2600 px per
m/s at sensitivity 1). Do not double-integrate to an absolute position; it
drifts within seconds. Jump: vertical linear acceleration
above 3.5 m/s^2, re-arm below 1.0 m/s^2, cooldown 0.6 s; count jumps with a
sequence number so the browser consumes each jump once. Use sensor
timestamps for dt.

5. Game
Serve the game on 127.0.0.1 only. Push velocity, accelerations, jump
counter, calibration state, packet statistics and sensor status to the
browser with Server-Sent Events at about 50 Hz. Accept POST requests only
with Content-Type application/json. Give each calibration request an id and
let the dialog react only to status messages with that id, so a stale
"ready" message does not close it early. If the HTTP port is busy, try the
next ones and open the browser on the port actually used.
Canvas 960x540, scaled to the window without horizontal scrolling. The world
scrolls left; the player moves with sensor velocity times a sensitivity
setting, clamped to the screen; arrow keys and Space also work. Ground blocks
to jump over, from level 2 falling rocks with a shadow warning to dodge
sideways, coins for +50. Score 10 points per second of active play, level up
every 15 s with faster scrolling and more obstacles, capped so jumps stay
possible. Collision ends the run.
Buttons: Start, Pause/Resume, Stop, Calibrate, Settings. Show score, level,
high score (saved in highscore.json next to the program), sensor status with
packet rate, a sideways acceleration and velocity meter, and a jump light.
If data is older than 500 ms while playing in sensor mode, pause and require
Resume. If no packets arrive 3 s after a successful configuration, show a
hint to check the PC IP and the firewall, or choose another UDP port.
Corporate Windows firewalls often block inbound UDP and ignore local rules,
or allow it only while the Ethernet network is classified as Private; then
use a port the policy allows (for example 30719 in our tests).

6. Tests and delivery
Unit-test the receiver with recorded real frames (good CRC, corrupted byte,
wrong start bytes) and the controller with synthetic samples: still sensor,
noise below the dead zone, push right/left, calibration learning a different
axis, invert, a tilted sensor that must not drift, a push while tilted,
an upward hop giving one jump, a sideways push giving no jump, and a shaky
calibration being rejected. Provide a PowerShell build script that runs the
tests and builds one console .exe with PyInstaller (--onefile, add the static
folder as data, pass the Kaitai folder with --paths and the generated modules
as hidden imports, name it picoScan150JumpAndRun). Include a README
with run, settings, calibration and firewall notes. Test with the real sensor
and state clearly what was verified with hardware.

docs.title: Native ROS 2 SLAM
docs.text:
Compatible with: picoScan100

Reliable localization is essential for autonomous driving, driverless-vehicle navigation, and a smooth material flow. High-resolution LiDAR measurements help map the surroundings. Localization software compares measurements with the map to estimate the vehicle's position and orientation, also called its pose. Accuracy depends on the environment, sensor setup, and software configuration.

Illustration of LiDAR mapping and localization with a mobile robot, occupancy map, and pose estimate.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
• How the native ROS 2 LaserScan topic of a picoScan150 feeds SLAM Toolbox.
  • The difference between mapping and localization, and why scan-matching odometry replaces wheel encoders here.
  • How to check the TF tree and the map-relative pose in RViz.

docs.title: ROS 2 for Beginners
docs.text:
For the simplest setup, run this example on an Ubuntu system supported by your ROS 2 distribution. ROS 2, SLAM Toolbox, and RViz are readily available as packages on supported Ubuntu releases. Match the Ubuntu version to the ROS 2 distribution's installation requirements.

ROS 2 is a software framework for connecting robot components. It is not a complete robot application: you combine programs called nodes to handle tasks such as receiving sensor data, estimating position, and driving motors. Nodes exchange messages over named topics.

For this example, a LiDAR integration publishes scan measurements. Mapping or localization software consumes those measurements together with robot motion information. Coordinate transforms (TF) describe how the sensor, robot, and map are positioned relative to one another.

docs.title: Mapping, Localization, and Navigation
docs.text:
Mapping, Localization, and Navigation: task and what it does.

Task What it does SLAM Simultaneous localization and mapping: builds a map while estimating the robot's pose. Localization Estimates the robot's pose within an existing map. Navigation Uses the pose and a destination to plan and follow a route while considering obstacles.

This example only builds a map and estimates the vehicle's pose within it. Use SLAM Toolbox for both stages: first run mapping, then load the saved pose graph in localization mode. A navigation stack, route planner, and motion controller are not required for this example.

docs.title: Suggested Data Path
docs.text:
The typical data path is:

LiDAR LaserScan → scan-matching odometry + TF → SLAM Toolbox → map-relative pose in RViz

This example uses LiDAR scan matching to estimate movement, without wheel encoders. Run a separate scan-matching odometry node alongside SLAM Toolbox; excluding encoders does not remove SLAM Toolbox's odometry requirement. Provide a suitable LaserScan topic to both nodes.

docs.title: Example Solution
docs.text: LiDAR mapping and localization example with ROS 2 and SLAM Toolbox.

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
• ros2 topic list shows the scan topic of the sensor.
  • In RViz, the map grows while you move the sensor slowly, and walls stay sharp instead of doubling.
  • In localization mode with the saved pose graph, the pose follows the sensor and the map does not shift.

docs.title: Project Prompt
docs.text:
Expand to view the project prompt 
Help me with a beginner-friendly ROS 2 handheld mapping
project, primarily on Linux, with Windows supported where feasible. Ask for
my OS/version and ROS distribution first. A reference implementation was tested
on Kilted, but do not require migration from a compatible working installation.
Assume I am starting from scratch without an existing repository, configuration,
dependency patches or helper scripts. Prefer compatible ROS binary packages on
Linux; build from source only when necessary. Record dependency versions or
pinned commits and preserve any required patches. Keep the architecture
OS-neutral and clearly label platform-specific install, build and activation
commands. Create any required launch files, configuration, tests and helper
scripts, and explain where to put them.

A SICK picoScan150 publishes native ROS 2 (DDS) LaserScan directly; do not add
a host-side SICK driver. I move the scanner by hand without wheel odometry.
Use RF2O scan odometry, SLAM Toolbox mapping and RViz to show live scans, a
growing occupancy map and the moving sensor pose. Use
https://sickag.github.io/sick_lidar_developer_guide/ for integration facts.

Verify firmware and license, Cyclone DDS, network interface,
discovery/domain, actual full single-echo LaserScan topic, QoS, frame,
angular geometry and acquisition timestamps. Discover values rather than
inventing settings or reusing another sensor's topic/frame blindly.

Preserve native scan timestamps. For standalone handheld mapping, publish
acquisition time on /handheld/clock, remap /clock and use_sim_time consistently
in RF2O, SLAM and RViz. Isolate motion TF on /handheld/tf and
/handheld/tf_static; exclude the sensor's identity world transform. Use the
observed laser frame as the handheld base, without an invented mounting TF.
RF2O owns handheld_odom -> laser; SLAM owns map -> handheld_odom. This
dedicated clock does not synchronize hardware clocks: do not connect robot
odometry, other sensors or Nav2 without verifying real clock alignment.

Verify RF2O handles asymmetric angular coverage, a valid initial quaternion,
invalid ranges, identical stationary scans, stable startup geometry and
strictly increasing timestamps. Reject incompatible geometry and report
failed matches instead of publishing stale poses. Verify SLAM accepts
translation OR in-place rotation with correct angle units. On Windows,
verify binary-mode pose-graph serialization and required native build fixes.
Check the installed versions before applying patches; do not duplicate fixes
already present upstream.

Deliver working launch/configuration and reproducible setup, not only proposed
commands. Automate SLAM lifecycle activation, prevent duplicate mapping
sessions and shut down if a critical process exits.
Explain environment activation, startup, Ctrl+C shutdown,
fresh-map restart, graph save and reload. Preserve both .posegraph and .data;
distinguish saved-pose-graph SLAM Toolbox localization from occupancy-grid
AMCL. Do not assume archive compatibility across versions or platforms.

docs.title: Reversing Assistant
docs.text:
Compatible with: picoScan100

When reversing a vehicle, objects behind it can be difficult to see and the available stopping distance decreases quickly. A LiDAR sensor can monitor this area and provide an immediate warning: the closer the nearest obstacle is, the faster the sensor LEDs flash.

The LiDAR monitors the reversing area. A shorter distance to the nearest obstacle produces a faster warning flash.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• Connect the picoScan150 and the development computer to the same network.
  • Mount the sensor so its field of view covers the monitored reversing area.
  • Build and install sick_perception_sdk with the picoScan100 examples.
  • Change receiverAddress if the computer does not use 192.168.0.100.
  • Set the environment variable SICK_PASSWORD to the Service password. The default passwords are documented in the operating instructions of your device. Do not pass them on, and change them during commissioning.

docs.title: Minimal Example
docs.text:
This example is based on the SDK's UDP streaming example. The point-cloud callback only calculates the flash period; the main loop performs the REST writes so scan reception is not blocked by an HTTP request.

The warning uses the radial range supplied by the scanner in the Compact scan data. Every point in the received frame is considered.

This example is adapted from the sick_perception_sdk UDP streaming example and is licensed under the MIT License. The upstream copyright and permission notice applies to copies or substantial portions of this example:

Expand to view the complete C++ example 
#include <sick_perception_sdk/compact_format/PointCloud/UnorganizedPointCloud.hpp>
#include <sick_perception_sdk/drivers/picoScan100/PicoScan100Driver.hpp>
#include <sick_perception_sdk/sensor_configuration/HttpClient/httplib_client/HttpClient.hpp>
#include <sick_perception_sdk/sensor_configuration/picoScan150/PicoScan150Configurator.hpp>

#include <atomic>
#include <algorithm>
#include <chrono>
#include <csignal>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <limits>
#include <memory>
#include <thread>

// The signal handler changes this flag when the user presses Ctrl+C.
std::atomic<bool> running {true};

int main()
{
  // Change these addresses if the sensor or computer uses another subnet.
  constexpr char sensorAddress[] = "192.168.0.1";
  sick::IpV4Address receiverAddress {"192.168.0.100"};
  constexpr std::uint16_t scanPort = 2115;

  // Read the Service password from the environment instead of the source code.
  char const* password = std::getenv("SICK_PASSWORD");
  if (password == nullptr)
  {
    return 1;
  }

  auto const httpClient =
    std::make_shared<sick::httplib_client::HttpClient>(sensorAddress, 80);
  sick::picoScan150::v2_3_3::Configurator configurator(
    httpClient, sick::UserLevel::Service, password);

  configurator.enableScanDataStreamingCompactUdp(receiverAddress, scanPort);

  // The scan callback writes these values while the main loop reads them.
  std::atomic<int> flashPeriodMs {0};
  std::atomic<std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point> lastFrame {
    std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point {}};

  // Request the scanner-provided radial range for every point.
  sick::point_cloud::PointCloudConfiguration pointCloudConfig;
  pointCloudConfig.fields.enableSpherical = true;

  sick::picoScan100::Driver driver;
  driver.scanDataReceiver()
    .setup(scanPort)
    .setOnNewFrameCallback(
      [&](sick::point_cloud::UnorganizedPointCloud const& cloud) {
        // Find the closest valid radial range in the complete scan frame.
        float nearest = std::numeric_limits<float>::infinity();
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < cloud.numberOfPoints(); ++i)
        {
          nearest = std::min(nearest, cloud.getRange(i));
        }

        // Store one full LED on/off period for the selected warning level.
        flashPeriodMs =
          nearest <= 0.5F ? 333 :
          nearest <= 2.0F ? 500 :
          nearest < std::numeric_limits<float>::infinity() ? 2000 : 0;
        lastFrame = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
      },
      pointCloudConfig);
  driver.run();

  std::signal(SIGINT, [](int) { running = false; });
  bool ledOn = false;
  while (running)
  {
    // Treat missing scan data as "no obstacle" after 500 ms.
    bool const scanIsCurrent =
      std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - lastFrame.load() <=
      std::chrono::milliseconds(500);
    int const period = scanIsCurrent ? flashPeriodMs.load() : 0;

    if (period == 0)
    {
      if (ledOn)
      {
        configurator.setLEDEnable(false);
        ledOn = false;
      }
      std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(50));
      continue;
    }

    // Toggling after half a period produces the requested flash frequency.
    ledOn = !ledOn;
    configurator.setLEDEnable(ledOn);
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(period / 2));
  }

  configurator.setLEDEnable(true);
}

Add the source as another picoScan100 example target and link it with sick_perception_sdk::drivers and sick_perception_sdk::sensor_configuration, like the SDK's data_streaming_udp example. Stop it with Ctrl+C; the final call enables the LEDs again, which is their default state.

docs.title: Expected Behavior
docs.text:
If no scan frame arrives for 500 ms, the scan is treated as stale and the LEDs are switched off.

Expected Behavior: nearest point, flash frequency, and result.

Nearest point Flash frequency Result No obstacle or stale scan Off LEDs stay off 0 m to 0.5 m 3 Hz Fast warning More than 0.5 m to 2 m 2 Hz Medium warning More than 2 m 0.5 Hz Slow warning

Move a test object through the sensor's field of view and check that the reported behavior changes monotonically: every smaller distance must produce the same or a shorter period. Test only in a controlled area; this example is a warning aid, not a safety function.

docs.title: Optional Digital Output
docs.text: The same ledOn value can be sent to POST /api/SetOutput at the same cadence. First configure that output's source as SOPAS command, then call the SDK's setOutput() method with the output number and value. Do not use OutputState for this: that endpoint only reads the current output states.

docs.title: ROS 2 Reversing Assistant with an Ambient-Light Image
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan200

This Level 3 project combines a multiScan270, an SDK-based ROS 2 wrapper, asynchronous field status, and an ambient-light view in RViz or another ROS-connected display.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
• How to wrap sick_perception_sdk data as ROS 2 topics over Zenoh.
  • How to combine WebSocket field events with REST field-group selection.
  • How to show the ambient-light image next to the point cloud in RViz.

docs.title: Application Background
docs.text:
A reversing assistant should show the area behind a vehicle and indicate whether the selected monitoring field is occupied. The operator switches between a close-range field for confined spaces and a wider monitoring field. The display must show the confirmed group, not just the requested mode.

Application illustration: an obstacle warning and a view of the reversing area help the driver assess the situation.

The multiScan270 provides a grayscale ambient-light image, not an RGB camera stream. Publish it as a ROS image so a display can show it alongside the point cloud and field status.

Ambient-light image example supplied for this project. The same type of image can be streamed through a ROS Image topic to RViz or a vehicle display; this picture is illustrative, not a capture from the current live session.

This prototype is a warning aid, not a safety function. Do not connect it to braking, steering, or motion authorization. Missing data, inactive fields, and disconnected communication must appear unavailable, never as a clear reversing area.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• Use a supported ROS 2 installation with compatible rmw_zenoh_cpp, RViz, colcon, and C++17 build tools. The architecture does not require a particular ROS distribution; match compiler, Python, and runtime libraries to your installation.
  • Use SDK 2.0.0 or a compatible newer release with the multiScan200 driver. Keep SDK build and dependency setup separate from the ROS workspace.
  • Configure the two existing fields in different TELEGRAM-controlled groups. Follow Field Evaluation rather than recreating the configuration procedure here. Record evaluation IDs, group IDs, and result-list positions separately; confirm which volume is near/wide.
  • Enable ambient data in Compact type 6 without overwriting other output options. Check compactTelegramType6Content in the multiScan200 REST reference.
  • Use the WebSocket Events registration pattern for FieldEvaluationResult; verify support on the target device. Offer compression, but do not require it when the server does not negotiate it.

Configuration example: retain the existing field geometry and assign each monitoring volume to its own selectable group.

Field-group example: name the group Close Range and select Telegram activation so the application can control it. Initially active defines its startup state; the screenshot shows it enabled. Configure the wide-range field in a separate group and verify both groups' startup states before selecting a mode.

docs.title: Suggested Data Path
docs.text:
Unlike native ROS 2 integration, this approach receives Compact data through the host SDK and publishes ROS messages itself. Zenoh transports those messages; it does not replace the device's TCP, WebSocket, or REST interfaces.

flowchart TD
    sensor["multiScan270"]
    sdk["SDK scan/image node"]
    events["Field status/control node"]
    ros["ROS 2 over Zenoh"]
    display["RViz or vehicle display"]
    sensor -->|"Compact TCP"| sdk
    sensor -->|"WebSocket events"| events
    events -->|"REST group selection"| sensor
    sensor -->|"REST contour read"| events
    sdk -->|"Point cloud + ambient image"| ros
    events -->|"Field status + colored contour markers"| ros
    ros --> display

Reversing-assistant data path: the SDK publishes point clouds and ambient-light images, while a separate node handles field events and REST control. ROS 2 over Zenoh carries the data to RViz or a vehicle display.

The wrapper publishes points (PointCloud2), ambient_light (Image), field_states (both evaluations with validity/activity), field_markers (MarkerArray volumes colored by live state), and diagnostics under /sick_multiscan200_node. A select_field_group service selects near or wide, verifies REST success and group readback, then waits for a fresh event snapshot before declaring field results current.

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
• RViz shows the point cloud and the ambient-light image.
  • The field volumes are green while free and turn red when an object enters.
  • Calling select_field_group switches between near and wide, and the group readback matches the selection.

docs.title: Example Solution
docs.text:
RViz example: field volumes read through REST are overlaid on the SDK point cloud. Live field events color evaluation 1 green (FREE) and evaluation 2 red (INFRINGED); colors change with the reported state.

Use the following single prompt to build the wrapper in your own workspace. Its phases also separate the reusable scan/image wrapper from field control.

Expand the complete project prompt 
# Build an SDK-Based ROS 2 Reversing Assistant

Create an OS-neutral multiScan270 warning prototype. Use sick_perception_sdk
2.0.0 or a compatible newer release, not the sensor's native ROS publisher.
Use the installed ROS 2 distribution with matching rmw_zenoh_cpp and RViz;
do not require migration to a named distribution. Inspect the actual SDK
headers and device OpenAPI instead of guessing APIs or firmware capabilities.

## Phase 1: Workspace and Interfaces

Create a C++17 ament_cmake package sick_multiscan200_node for SDK reception
and custom ROS interfaces. Use a separate Python rclpy package
sick_multiscan200_events with an asyncio WebSocket/REST client so network
control never blocks scan callbacks. Deliver launch, YAML and RViz files.
Keep the SDK and ROS sources unchanged.

Parameters: sensor_address, scan_port (default 2115), frame_id (lidar),
mirror_image, publish_identity_tf (false), mapping_verified (false),
and separate near/wide evaluation IDs, group IDs and zero-based result indexes.
Validate all values. Require verified mapping before trusting field status
or enabling switching; do not infer group IDs from evaluation IDs.

Publish under /sick_multiscan200_node:
- points: sensor_msgs/PointCloud2
- ambient_light: sensor_msgs/Image
- field_states: custom FieldStateArray
- field_markers: visualization_msgs/MarkerArray
- diagnostics: diagnostic_msgs/DiagnosticArray
- select_field_group: custom service, string mode -> success/message/group ID

Each FieldState includes evaluation_id, group_id, raw_state, valid, active,
and reason. Use reliable KeepLast(5) for scan/image and reliable
transient-local KeepLast(1) for status. Report scan/image/event health separately.

## Phase 2: SDK Point Cloud

Use sick::multiScan200::Driver and scanDataReceiver().setup(scan_port).
Attach an explicitly typed UnorganizedPointCloud callback plus a raw
MultiScan200Data callback; the SDK multiplexes them. Enable Cartesian
coordinates, intensity, time offsets, ring, layer and echo indexes.

Map SDK fields/offsets/types to PointCloud2, preserve meter scaling and
sensor acquisition time, and validate sizes, byte counts and endian order.
ROS PointField has no Int64/Uint64: reject them or numerically repack;
never relabel integer bytes as FLOAT64. Handle timestamp overflow explicitly.

## Phase 3: Ambient Image and RViz

Read type-6 ambientLightData and its actual metadata dimensions. Convert
column-major samples to row-major mono16, with step=width*2 and explicit
little-endian bytes. Mirror horizontally only when mirror_image is enabled.
Preserve sensor time and raw pixel values. Reject malformed/partial frames;
skip missing image data with a diagnostic, never synthesize an image.

Configure RViz PointCloud2 and Image displays, reliable QoS and fixed frame
lidar. Normalize only the displayed image. Do not use Camera without
CameraInfo or invent calibration. Leave map-to-sensor identity TF disabled;
moving vehicles require real mounting/localization transforms and clock sync.

## Phase 4: Field Events and Group Selection

Register FieldEvaluationResult at ws://<sensor_address>/apievents using
the documented event envelope. Handle both initial registration data and
subsequent events. Offer permessage-deflate, accept an uncompressed session,
and explicitly report unsupported registration or malformed data.

Preserve raw device states. Only a current FREE result for a confirmed
active group is clear; inactive, unknown, disconnected or pending is not.
Keep transition states as warnings. Reconnect with bounded backoff,
resubscribe and invalidate old results until a fresh snapshot arrives.
A quiet healthy subscription is not automatically stale.

The near/wide service touches only the two configured groups. Serialize
requests, mark status pending, check HTTP and device response headers and
every activation result, then verify target active/other inactive by readback.
Do not assume switching is atomic. Discard old in-flight results and obtain
a fresh subscription snapshot after switching. Monitor external group
changes even while field events continue arriving.

Read each evaluation's contour and configuration through the REST API,
using the documented authentication without storing credentials in the
workspace. Convert polygon coordinates and lower/upper Z limits from
millimeters to meters in the sensor frame. Publish the actual field volumes
as RViz markers, with green for FREE, red for INFRINGED, amber for transition
states, gray for inactive and a distinct unknown indication on invalid or
disconnected data. Show evaluation IDs and state labels. Never invent
geometry when access is denied; report the error and request authentication.

## Phase 5: Build and Run

Provide Windows and Linux build/environment instructions, a combined launch
file, YAML configuration and RViz layout. Match SDK/ROS compiler runtimes
(including /MD on Windows) and stop/join workers cleanly on shutdown.
Start a Zenoh router and use the same middleware/domain in all terminals.
Do not create/delete fields, write EEPROM or change network settings.
Keep verification scripts, captures and test reports local, outside the guide.
Explain clock synchronization, field-mapping and scene-orientation checks.

docs.title: Run and Display
docs.text:
After building the generated packages, activate ROS and your workspace in every terminal. Select the same middleware and domain for all processes:

Windows PowerShellLinux 
$env:RMW_IMPLEMENTATION = "rmw_zenoh_cpp"
$env:ROS_DOMAIN_ID = "187"
ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION="rmw_zenoh_cpp"
export ROS_DOMAIN_ID="187"
ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

Use an available router endpoint and a domain appropriate for your system. In another activated terminal, launch with your edited YAML path; the launch file must load it for both nodes. In a third, open the generated RViz layout. These relative paths assume the generated workspace is the working directory:

ros2 launch sick_multiscan200_node multiscan200.launch.py \
  config:="$PWD/src/sick_multiscan200_node/config/reversing_assistant.yaml"
rviz2 -d src/sick_multiscan200_node/rviz/reversing_assistant.rviz

On PowerShell, use native paths and its continuation syntax instead:

ros2 launch sick_multiscan200_node multiscan200.launch.py `
  "config:=$PWD\src\sick_multiscan200_node\config\reversing_assistant.yaml"
rviz2 -d .\src\sick_multiscan200_node\rviz\reversing_assistant.rviz

The Image display subscribes to /sick_multiscan200_node/ambient_light. A custom vehicle display can subscribe to that same topic. Keep Fixed Frame at lidar for the stationary example; the ambient view is not a calibrated overlay on the point cloud.

Inspect status and request a group using the generated interfaces:

ros2 topic echo --once /sick_multiscan200_node/field_states
ros2 service call /sick_multiscan200_node/select_field_group \
  sick_multiscan200_node/srv/SelectFieldGroup "{mode: near}"

ros2 service call /sick_multiscan200_node/select_field_group `
  sick_multiscan200_node/srv/SelectFieldGroup "{mode: wide}"

Confirm the returned group and current field status. Before vehicle use, check actual near/wide geometry, sensor clock synchronization and image orientation with an asymmetric scene. Do not change a working installation or persistent sensor settings merely to follow the example.

docs.title: Smart Shelf
docs.text:
Compatible with: picoScan100

Smart shelves record which compartment goods are taken from or put into. A 2D LiDAR scans a light curtain in front of the rack. The sensor evaluates the data itself and reports where the curtain is crossed. Software turns this position into a compartment and checks if the pick was correct.

Smart shelf: the scan plane in front of the rack shows where a hand reaches in.

In this project, a picoScan stands in front of a desktop monitor. The browser draws a shelf on the screen. Touch a compartment with a pen and it lights up.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
• How on-device perpendicular distance turns the scan plane into a light curtain.
  • How a browser receives sensor events directly over WebSocket.
  • How a three-point teach-in maps sensor coordinates to screen positions.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• A picoScan, for example picoScan150, on the same network as your computer (Getting Started).
  • A browser. No server, Python or SICK SDK is needed.
  • Place the picoScan on the desk at the lower-left edge of the monitor so the scan plane runs just in front of the screen.

docs.title: Solution Path
docs.text:
Perpendicular distance on the sensor → WebSocket event → pen position → compartment → dwell time → pick check

  1. Set up Perpendicular Distance Measurement with a field that covers the screen. Use a small minimum object size, for example 10 mm, so a pen is detected.
  2. The browser subscribes to perpendicularDistanceResult on ws://192.168.0.1/apievents (WebSocket Events).
  3. The middle of the minimum and maximum distance positions is the pen position in millimeters.
  4. A three-point teach-in maps sensor millimeters to screen pixels.
  5. The pen must stay in one compartment for 150 ms to count as a pick.

Setup: the picoScan stands at the lower-left screen edge and scans just in front of the screen. The laser beam measures in polar coordinates; the sensor reports the perpendicular distance d to a horizontal reference line.

Perpendicular distance field in SOPASair. The field covers the screen in front of the sensor.

The browser connects to the sensor directly. It registers once and then gets an event each time the result changes:

{"type": "register", "event": "perpendicularDistanceResult", "clientId": 1}

Register message for the perpendicular distance result.

Each event carries one entry per evaluation. Distances and positions are in millimeters:

{
  "type": "event",
  "event": "perpendicularDistanceResult",
  "clientId": 1,
  "status": 0,
  "data": {
    "perpendicularDistanceResult": {
      "timestamp": 4773260000,
      "evaluations": [
        {
          "evaluationId": 1,
          "minimumDistance": 176,
          "maximumDistance": 184,
          "minimumDistancePosition": {"x": 318, "y": -176, "z": 0},
          "maximumDistancePosition": {"x": 322, "y": -184, "z": 0}
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}

Example event with a pen in the field. The pen position is the middle of both positions: x 320 mm, y −180 mm.

  • minimumDistance and maximumDistance are the smallest and largest perpendicular distances to the reference line inside the field.
  • minimumDistancePosition and maximumDistancePosition are the scan points with these distances, in sensor coordinates.
  • The register reply has the same data and already holds the current result.

An empty field reports all distances and positions as zero. The app treats this as "no object".

Smart shelf in the browser: the blue compartment is the pick target, the yellow dot is the pen.

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
• Without a sensor, a mouse drag over a compartment lights it up.
  • With the sensor, the status shows "Connected" and the pen position updates when you touch the screen.
  • After the teach-in, the yellow dot sits under the pen tip.
  • A quick pass through a compartment does not count; holding the pen in one does.
  • In pick-to-light mode, the target flashes green and other compartments flash red.

docs.title: Project Prompt
docs.text:
Paste this prompt into your coding assistant in a new workspace. It asks for the browser app, tests and a README.

Expand to view the complete project prompt 
Build a beginner-friendly level-two project called "picoScan Smart Shelf".
A SICK picoScan100 stands at the lower edge of my desktop monitor. Its
perpendicular distance evaluation is already configured on the sensor and
covers the screen. The browser draws a shelf on the screen. When I touch a
compartment with a pen, the compartment lights up.
Deliver working files, not a plan. Work in a new folder outside the
developer guide. Use plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Canvas. No build
step, framework, server, Python or SICK SDK. Opening index.html must be
enough. Keep the code easy to follow.

Sensor data:
- Connect the browser directly to ws://<sensor-ip>/apievents. Default IP
  192.168.0.1. WebSockets need no CORS, so this works from file://.
- Send {"type":"register","event":"perpendicularDistanceResult",
  "clientId":1}. The register reply already contains the current result;
  handle it like an event. Reconnect after 2 s when the socket closes.
- Events only arrive when the result changes. Run dwell timing on a timer
  or animation frame, not only on incoming messages.
- Read data.perpendicularDistanceResult.evaluations and pick the entry with
  the configured evaluationId (default 1). Use the middle of
  minimumDistancePosition and maximumDistancePosition (x, y in mm) as the
  pen position. If both positions are 0,0, the field is empty.
- Do not call the REST API from the browser. It sends no CORS headers.

Shelf:
- Draw a shelf with uprights, boards and labeled bins (A1, A2 ... with row A
  at the top). Default 3 rows x 4 columns, filling the canvas.
- Default mapping: the field rectangle x -100..600 mm, y -400..0 mm fills
  the canvas; screen up is negative y.
- Add a teach-in: show three crosshair targets near the top-left,
  top-right and bottom-left corners. I hold the pen on each target. Accept
  a point when it stays within 15 mm for 700 ms and average the samples.
  I must lift the pen before the next target. Esc cancels. Solve an affine
  transform from the three points so any rotation or mirroring works.
  After teach-in, ignore sensor input until the pen is lifted.
- A pick is one visit to a compartment that lasts at least the dwell time
  (default 150 ms). A quick pass through a compartment is not a pick.
- Show the live pen as a yellow dot and outline its compartment. Count
  picks per compartment.
- Toolbar: connection status, pen position and compartment, score, and
  buttons for start picking, teach corners, settings and full screen.
- Settings dialog: sensor IP, evaluation ID, rows, columns, dwell time and
  the field rectangle. Store settings and the teach-in in localStorage.
  Warn if the window size changed since the teach-in.

Put parsing, the affine transform, the compartment lookup and the pick
detector in one pure module and test it with node:test. Include a README
with setup, teach-in and test commands. If you add a Python test client,
disable WebSocket keepalive pings; the sensor does not answer them. Test
with the real sensor and state clearly what was verified with hardware.

docs.title: Choose a Configuration Option
docs.text:
Start with the REST interface: it covers reading and writing parameters for applications and scripts. The other options cover legacy integrations, configuration files, security, and interactive testing.

  • REST Interface: use the HTTP/JSON API to read and write parameters or call device methods from applications and scripts. Writes require challenge-response authentication.
  • CoLa Interface: send SICK commands and telegrams, especially for PLCs, legacy integrations, or systems already using CoLa.
  • Backup & Restore: save, recover, or deploy a complete configuration file; restore only to a matching device type.
  • HTTPS & Certificates: protect REST traffic with TLS and let clients verify the sensor using a trusted certificate.
  • Third-Party Tools: import OpenAPI into Insomnia or Postman to explore endpoints and test requests interactively.

Insomnia and Postman are clients of the REST interface, not separate device protocols.

docs.title: CoLa Interface
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

CoLa (Command Language) is SICK's telegram protocol for reading and writing sensor parameters, calling methods, and subscribing to events over TCP. Use it for PLCs and existing SICK integrations; for new integrations, prefer the REST API.

CoLa Interface: variant, encoding, TCP port, framing, and checksum.

Variant Encoding TCP port Framing Checksum CoLa A ASCII 2111 <STX> … <ETX> (02 … 03) None CoLa B Binary 2112 02 02 02 02 + 4-byte big-endian length 1-byte XOR

On picoScan100, CoLa A and CoLa B (together called CoLa1) can be disabled for security; see Cybersecurity.

docs.title: Command Basics
docs.text:
Every telegram starts with a command type, followed by a space and the command name. The device answers with the matching answer type:

Command Basics: command type, request, answer, and hex value of the request.

Command type Request Answer Request in hex Read a variable sRN sRA 73 52 4E Write a variable sWN sWA 73 57 4E Call a method sMN sAN 73 4D 4E Register for an event sEN sEA, then sSN per event 73 45 4E

An error is answered with sFA and an error code.

The framing differs between the two variants:

Command Basics: framing element, CoLa A, and CoLa B.

Element CoLa A (ASCII) CoLa B (binary) Start <STX> = 02 02 02 02 02 + 4-byte length End <ETX> = 03 1-byte XOR checksum Separator {SPC} = 20 20 after the command name only

If values are divided into two parts (e.g. measurement data), they are documented according to LSB 0 (e.g. 00 07), output however is according to MSB (e.g. 07 00).

docs.title: ASCII Telegram (CoLa A)
docs.text:
CoLa A is the plain-text alternative. It is convenient for manual tests and parametrization. For PLCs, CoLa B is still recommended because CoLa A telegrams have a variable length.

A CoLa A telegram has two parts: the framing and the data part. <STX> (02) starts and <ETX> (03) ends each telegram.

The data part contains the command in plain text, then the parameter values. Values are hexadecimal by default, or decimal with a leading +. Fixed values with a specific meaning are always hexadecimal. Example: 25 Hz = +2500 (decimal) = 9C4 (hex).

Leading zeros are removed in CoLa A, so a space is required between every command part and every parameter.

Without the + sign, a numeric parameter is read as hexadecimal. For single digits 0-9 this makes no difference, but from 10 upwards it does: 10 and 010 are both read as 0x10 = 16, while +10 is decimal 10. Write every decimal value greater than 9 with a leading + (for example +10, +48, +2500).

You can also send the whole telegram as hex bytes, converting every character, including digits, through the ASCII table.

The device always answers with parameter values in hexadecimal, regardless of the format you sent.

Example: ASCII telegram

ASCII Telegram (CoLa A): format, start, data, and stop.

Format Start Data Stop ASCII <STX> sMN{SPC}SetAccessMode{SPC}03{SPC}<password hash> <ETX> Hex 02 73 4D 4E 20 53 65 74 41 63 63 65 73 73 4D 6F 64 65 20 30 33 20 <password hash> 03

This is again an example telegram for setting the user level "Authorized Client". As only fixed hexadecimal parameter values are needed, the option to use parameter values in decimal code with special indicator cannot be applied here:

  • Framing = <STX> = telegram start = 02 (Hex)
  • Data:
  • sMN = start of SOPAS command (and blank) = 73 4D 4E 20 (Hex)
  • SetAccessMode = the actual command for setting the user level (and blank) = 53 65 74 41 63 63 65 73 73 4D 6F 64 65 20 (Hex)
  • 03 = fixed Hex value meaning user level "Authorized Client" (and blank) = 30 33 20 (Hex)
  • <password hash> = 8 hex characters: the hash of the password for the selected user level
  • Framing = <ETX> = telegram stop = 03 (Hex)

The default passwords are documented in the operating instructions of your device. Do not pass them on, and change them during commissioning.

docs.title: Binary Telegram (CoLa B)
docs.text:
A CoLa B telegram has four parts: header, data length, data, and checksum. All values are bytes, shown in hexadecimal. CoLa B is recommended for PLCs: the transmitted data is about half the size of CoLa A, and the length field makes parsing simple.

  • Header: four STX bytes, 02 02 02 02.
  • Data length: 4 bytes, big-endian, the number of bytes in the data part. The maximum is 2³² − 1 = 4,294,967,295 bytes.
  • Data: the command as ASCII bytes, followed by the parameters as binary values. There is always a space (20) between the command and the parameters, but not between parameter values.
  • Checksum: 1 byte, the XOR of all bytes in the data part.

Example: Binary telegram

Binary Telegram (CoLa B): component and value.

Component Value Header 02 02 02 02 Length 00 00 00 17 Data 73 4D 4E 20 53 65 74 41 63 63 65 73 73 4D 6F 64 65 20 03 <password hash> CS XOR of the data bytes

This is an example telegram for setting the user level "Authorized Client":

  • Header = 02 02 02 02
  • Length = 23 bytes (17h)
  • Data:
  • 73 4D 4E 20 = sMN = start of SOPAS command (and space)
  • 53 65 74 41 63 63 65 73 73 4D 6F 64 65 20 = SetAccessMode = the actual command for setting the user level (and space)
  • 03 = fixed Hex value meaning user level "Authorized Client"
  • <password hash> = 4 bytes: the hash of the password for the selected user level
  • Checksum = the XOR of all 23 data bytes

docs.title: Validate a CoLa B Checksum
docs.text:
CoLa B is transported over TCP, so one TCP read is not necessarily one complete telegram. Buffer incoming bytes, locate the four-byte sync header, read the following 4-byte big-endian payload length, and wait until the complete frame has arrived. The frame consists of the 8-byte header and length, the payload, and one checksum byte; therefore its total size is 9 + payload_length.

The checksum is the XOR of every payload byte, excluding the sync header, length field, and checksum byte. For a complete frame in a byte array frame, calculate it as follows:

xor_sum = 0
for byte in frame[8:-1]:
    xor_sum ^= byte

checksum_valid = xor_sum == frame[-1]
Show full Python checksum example

The following dummy LMDscandata response is an example captured from a picoScan150 with firmware V2.1.0. It demonstrates frame separation and XOR validation; it contains a small number of beams and is not a production measurement sample. The length bytes in this sample are 00 00 00 77, which encode a 119-byte payload in big-endian order. The checksum is BB.

tcp_payload = [
    0x02, 0x02, 0x02, 0x02, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x77,
    0x73, 0x52, 0x41, 0x20, 0x4c, 0x4d, 0x44, 0x73,
    0x63, 0x61, 0x6e, 0x64, 0x61, 0x74, 0x61, 0x20,
    0x00, 0x01, 0x00, 0x01, 0x01, 0x64, 0x72, 0x18,
    0x00, 0x00, 0x59, 0x89, 0x69, 0x97, 0xbb, 0x9d,
    0xc5, 0x02, 0xbb, 0x9e, 0x82, 0xcc, 0x00, 0x00,
    0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x05, 0xdc,
    0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x01,
    0x44, 0x49, 0x53, 0x54, 0x31, 0x40, 0x00, 0x00,
    0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x0d, 0xe2,
    0xb0, 0x13, 0x88, 0x00, 0x03, 0x00, 0x00, 0x3a,
    0xdb, 0x3a, 0xda, 0x00, 0x01, 0x52, 0x53, 0x53,
    0x49, 0x31, 0x3f, 0x80, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00,
    0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x0d, 0xe2, 0xb0, 0x13, 0x88,
    0x00, 0x03, 0x00, 0x35, 0x39, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00,
    0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0xbb,
]

xor_sum = 0
for byte in tcp_payload[8:-1]:
    xor_sum ^= byte

if xor_sum == tcp_payload[-1]:
    print("Checksum valid")
else:
    print("Checksum invalid")

docs.title: Device-Specific Telegram Listing
docs.text:
For device-specific commands and parameter telegrams, see the LRS4000 Telegram Listing, multiScan100 Telegram Listing, multiScan200 Telegram Listing, and picoScan100 Telegram Listing.

Every write command (sWN) has a read (sRN) counterpart, even if the Telegram Listing does not describe it. Use it to verify the current value, for example read the IP address with sRN EIIpAddr.

docs.title: Variable Types
docs.text:
Variable Types: variable type, length, value range, and sign.

Variable type Length (byte) Value range Sign Bool_1 1 0 or 1 No Uint_8 1 0 … 255 No Int_8 1 -128 … +127 Yes Uint_16 2 0 … 65,535 No Int_16 2 -32,768 … +32,767 Yes Uint_32 4 0 … 4,294,967,295 No Int_32 4 -2,147,483,648 … +2,147,483,647 Yes ULInt_64 8 0 … 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 No Enum_8 1 Certain values defined in a list of Choices (0 … 255) No Enum_16 2 Certain values defined in a list of Choices (0 … 65535) No String Context-dependent Strings are not terminated in zeroes FlexString array of visible characters with preceding current length(UInt length) (array of 8 bit) See description of String and FlexArray Real 4 Float according to IEEE 754 (see the IEEE 754 converter) Yes

Data length is always given in bytes.

Variable Types: compound type and description.

Type Description Struct A structure is a sequence of further types. These types can be of a BasicType, Structs again or an Array. Array An Array is a repetition of a type. The length of the array is defined with each Array. The types can be of a BasicType, a Struct or an Array again (n-dimensional). Flex Array A FlexArray is a repetition of a type with a variable length. The maximum length of the array is defined with each FlexArray. The current length of the FlexArray is transferred as a UInt preceding the Array itself. The types can be of a BasicType, a Struct or an Array again (n-dimensional).

docs.title: CoLa Error Codes
docs.text:
An sFA response reports a SOPAS error. The error code is returned as a decimal value in CoLa A and as a hexadecimal value in CoLa B.

CoLa Error Codes: symbol, description, decimal, and hexadecimal value.

Symbol Description Dec. Hex. Sopas_Ok No error 0 0 Sopas_Error_METHODIN_ACCESSDENIED Wrong user level; access to the method is not allowed 1 1 Sopas_Error_METHODIN_UNKNOWNINDEX Method index is unknown 2 2 Sopas_Error_VARIABLE_UNKNOWNINDEX Variable index is unknown 3 3 Sopas_Error_LOCALCONDITIONFAILED A local condition was violated, such as a value outside the allowed range 4 4 Sopas_Error_INVALID_DATA Invalid variable data;
