This calculator requires JavaScript.

Device and Compact Output

Estimated Result

Loading the calculator…

Remarks:

  • The calculator provides an estimate of bandwidth requirements. It considers scan data and selected IMU or encoder telegrams, but not additional configuration traffic.
  • Ensure that your network infrastructure can handle the estimated bandwidth to avoid data loss or latency issues.

docs.title: Filter Details
docs.text:
Filters run on the sensor and change the measurement data before it is sent. Use them to reduce bandwidth, remove unwanted points, and keep the data your application needs. The available filters and their settings differ between devices; each section lists the devices it applies to.

Filter Details: filter, effect, side effect, and devices.

Filter Effect Side effect Devices Interval Sends only every n-th scan Lower output rate multiScan100, multiScan200, picoScan150 Fog Removes fog echoes at close range - multiScan100, picoScan150 Echo Selects which echoes are sent - LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, picoScan150 Particle Removes dust, rain, and snow hits Device-specific settings and latency LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, picoScan100 Moving average Averages distances over several scans Delayed output multiScan100, multiScan200, picoScan150 Blooming Removes blooming artifacts next to highly reflective objects - multiScan200 Angle range Limits horizontal output; multiScan200 also supports vertical ROI Partly masked Compact segments retain their size multiScan100, multiScan200, picoScan150 Layer Removes complete scan layers from the output Reduced vertical coverage multiScan100 Vertical FoV Keeps nested vertical regions at different resolutions Raw stream only multiScan200 Angle range focus Keeps a 3D angle range with an optional full-resolution region Raw stream only multiScan200 Rectangular Keeps points inside an X/Y rectangle Other points set to 0; data size unchanged multiScan100, picoScan150 Distance Keeps points inside a radial range Other points set to 0; data size unchanged LRS4000, multiScan100, picoScan150 Ground Filters ground returns with configurable thresholds Variant and configuration dependent multiScan100 Sensitivity mode Trades receiver sensitivity against robustness Higher sensitivity adds noise in ambient light LRS4000, multiScan200, picoScan150 Mean and median Median removes outliers; mean averages over several scans. Settings LFPmedianfilter and MeanFilter in the OpenAPI Delayed output LRS4000

Active filters run one after another, each on the result of the previous one, in this order:

Filter Details: device and filter processing order.

Device Processing order LRS4000 Particle → echo → median → mean multiScan100 Fog → echo → particle → moving average → data reduction multiScan200 Echo → particle → interval → blooming → angle range (details) picoScan100 Fog → echo → particle → moving average → data reduction and region of interest

Each active filter adds processing time and therefore output latency. For exact parameter names and value ranges, see the product's OpenAPI reference: LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, or picoScan100.

docs.title: Interval Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The interval filter reduces the scan output rate by a configurable reduction factor from 2 to 50. For example, a factor of three outputs only every third scan, reducing the output rate to one third. On picoScan100, this REST setting is exposed by the picoScan150 OpenAPI.

docs.title: Fog Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 picoScan100

The fog filter removes unwanted echoes at close range (approximately 3 m). This reduces false activations in fog. On picoScan100, this REST setting is exposed by the picoScan150 OpenAPI. The multiScan200 has no configurable fog filter.

docs.title: Echo Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The echo filter suppresses measurement data caused by edge hits, rain, dust, snow, and other ambient conditions. Pulses attributed to undesirable ambient conditions are not output. The selectable echoes differ by device:

Echo Filter: device and selectable echoes.

Device Selectable echoes picoScan150 First echo, last echo, or all echoes multiScan200 First echo, last echo, strongest echo, all echoes, or all echoes with the strongest first LRS4000, multiScan100 Read the selectable echo options for the installed firmware in the device's OpenAPI description.

On the multiScan200, field evaluation always uses a single echo. If all echoes are selected, field evaluation uses the first echo.

Example of retaining or suppressing an echo caused by ambient conditions.

picoScan100 example: Use multi-echo to suppress a glass-pane return and retain measurements of objects behind it.

docs.title: Particle Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The particle filter suppresses small, irrelevant reflection pulses caused by dust, raindrops, snowflakes, and similar particles. The filter settings differ by device.

Particle Filter: device and settings.

Device Settings LRS4000 On/off and a distance-step threshold from 500 to 5000 mm multiScan100 On/off and a distance-step threshold from 20 to 5000 mm multiScan200 On/off, a distance threshold from 20 to 2000 mm, and the minimum number of neighbors from 0 to 8 picoScan100 On/off and a distance-step threshold from 20 to 5000 mm

For LRS4000, multiScan100, and picoScan100, the threshold is the required distance step between the echo to be filtered and the echoes of surrounding beam angles. On multiScan200, a point needs at least the configured number of neighboring measurements within the distance threshold. In interlaced multiScan200 scan configurations (10 to 12), the filter compares measurements from different angular positions, so its effect can change. In the Compact format (telegram type 6), bit 6 of the multiScan200 echo properties marks points detected as particles.

docs.title: Moving Average Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

On picoScan150, the moving average filter smooths distance values by calculating the arithmetic mean over several scans of the same point. Configure an averaging depth of two to four scans. The first value is output only after the configured number of scans; invalid distance values (0) are excluded from the average.

Example of a four-scan moving average for representative angular positions (distance values in mm):

Moving Average Filter: scan/output, angle 3, angle 4, angle 5, angle 6, angle 7, and angle 8.

Scan/output Angle 3 Angle 4 Angle 5 Angle 6 Angle 7 Angle 8 Scan 1 1100 1100 1150 1150 1380 1380 Scan 2 1200 1200 1190 950 1500 1500 Scan 3 1150 1450 1200 1200 1450 1450 Scan 4 1170 1170 1220 1220 1470 1150 1. Output (scans 1–4) 1155 1230 1190 1130 1450 1370 Scan 5 0 1110 1150 1150 1380 1380 2. Output (scans 2–5) 1173 1233 1190 1130 1450 1370 Scan 6 1200 1210 1190 0 1500 1500 3. Output (scans 3–6) 1173 1235 1190 1190 1450 1370 Scan 7 1150 0 1200 1200 1450 1450 4. Output (scans 4–7) 1173 1163 1190 1190 1450 1370

Individual outliers still influence the average. Invalid distance values (0) are excluded, so fewer scans contribute at those positions (for example angle 3 in the 2nd output: (1200 + 1150 + 1170) / 3 = 1173).

On multiScan200, the moving average filter is called high precision mode and can only be switched on or off. It averages the distance of each point over several scans, which reduces distance noise while the output rate stays the same. The output is delayed by about 0.5 s. If the distance of an object changes significantly, averaging stops for that object. Use it for static scenes only. It has no effect in interlaced scan configurations (10 to 12).

On multiScan100, the REST API exposes LFPmovingAveragingFilter. Check the OpenAPI description for the available averaging depth and limits for the installed firmware.

docs.title: Blooming Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan200

Highly reflective objects such as retroreflectors can create false points next to the object (blooming). The blooming filter removes them. Select the strength low, medium (default), or strong. In the Compact format (telegram type 6), bit 2 of the echo properties marks points detected as blooming.

docs.title: Angle Range Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The available angle range controls depend on the device. multiScan100 and picoScan150 use horizontal start/stop angles; multiScan100 uses the layer filter for vertical coverage. multiScan200 also supports vertical regions and focus settings. A beam increment subsamples the selected data.

Angle Range Filter: comparison criterion, multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan150.

multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan150 Horizontal range −180° to +180° −180° to +180° −138° to +138° Vertical range Use the layer filter −90° to +90° Not applicable (2D) Beam increment 1 to 20 1 to 50, separately for horizontal and vertical 1 to 20

Complete Compact segments outside the horizontal range are not transmitted. Partly selected segments can retain zero-filled measurements and their full byte size. The exact savings from subsampling, vertical ROI, and focus depend on the serialized layout; verify them in a capture. The ambient-light image is limited by the configured data-reduction settings too.

docs.title: Layer Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100

The multiScan100 layer filter removes complete scan layers from the output data. Configure one Boolean value per layer through LFPlayerFilter; only enabled layers are serialized. This reduces the data volume when an application needs only part of the sensor's vertical coverage. The filter changes the output, not the physical scan performed by the sensor.

docs.title: Vertical FoV Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan200

The multiScan200 CoLa command verticalAngleRangeFilter restricts raw streaming data to an outer vertical region of interest (ROI). An optional inner ROI must lie completely inside the outer ROI. Each region has its own layer increment from 1 to 50, so the inner region can retain more vertical detail while the surrounding region is subsampled more strongly. Layers outside the outer ROI are not transmitted.

The filter also limits ambient-light data. In Full mode, the remaining ambient-light region keeps its full vertical resolution. In Matching mode, its vertical resolution matches the primary measurement data, with one ambient-light pixel per beam.

docs.title: Angle Range Focus Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan200

The multiScan200 angleRangeFocusFilter restricts raw streaming data to a 3D field of view defined by horizontal (theta) and vertical (phi) limits. Beams outside this range are not transmitted. Separate horizontal and vertical increments from 1 to 50 can subsample the remaining data.

An optional focus region preserves full resolution inside a smaller horizontal or vertical region while the surrounding data remains subsampled. This filter affects raw data streaming only and does not affect field evaluation.

docs.title: Rectangular Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 picoScan100

After the measurement filters, data-reduction settings and the region of interest filter limit the points passed on for further processing. On picoScan100, this REST setting is exposed by the picoScan150 OpenAPI.

When the rectangular filter is active, only scan parts within the rectangle are retained. The filter does not reduce the data; points outside the rectangle are set to zero. Adjust the rectangle by setting the minimum and maximum X and Y values in millimeters.

docs.title: Distance Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 picoScan100

The distance filter limits the measured radial distance and therefore affects a circular area around the product. It does not reduce the data; points outside the selected radial range are set to zero. To keep a circular area, set the maximum range to the required radius in millimeters. To keep a ring, set the maximum range to the required radius and the minimum range to a value greater than 0 mm. On picoScan100, this REST setting is exposed by the picoScan150 OpenAPI.

docs.title: Ground Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100

The multiScan100 REST API exposes groundFilterEnable, groundFilterThresholds, and groundFilterType. The filter can reduce false field-evaluation triggers caused by the ground while retaining detection of small objects when configured correctly. The ground filter is not applied to the raw measurement-data streaming path. Availability can depend on the variant and software package. See multiScan100 release notes and the multiScan100 OpenAPI reference.

docs.title: Sensitivity Mode
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan200 picoScan100

The REST variable SensitivityMode sets the sensitivity of the receiver. A higher sensitivity increases the scanning range but also measurement noise, especially in ambient light. The LRS4000 offers 0 NORMAL, 1 INCREASED, and 2 HIGHEST. The multiScan200 and picoScan150 offer 0 MAXIMUM_ROBUSTNESS, 1 STANDARD (recommended), and 2 MAXIMUM_DETECTIVITY. For the ambient-light limits, see the LRS4000 release notes.

docs.title: LMDscandata Format
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 picoScan100

LMDscandata is a scan data telegram of SICK's CoLa interface. LRS4000 and picoScan100 expose it as a selectable scan data format. On picoScan100 it is sent over a TCP connection that the client opens to the sensor, so delivery is ordered and error-checked. Use it for PLCs and integrations that already use CoLa. For new high-rate integrations, use Compact or MSGPACK over the transport supported by the device.

docs.title: Receive LMDscandata
docs.text:
1. Select LMDscandata as the measurement data output format (sWN ScanDataFormat, or in SOPASair under Application > Data output).
  2. Open a TCP connection to the sensor: port 2111 for CoLa A or 2112 for CoLa B.
  3. Request data:

Receive LMDscandata: telegram and result.

Telegram Result sRN LMDscandata Returns one scan (polling) sEN LMDscandata 1 Starts continuous output: one telegram per scan sEN LMDscandata 0 Stops continuous output

No data is sent during boot-up or in some error states (for example Device Not Ready). A login session does not block the output. RSSI in LMDscandata is 8-bit; the value 254 marks a detected reflector.

If the output format is not set to LMDscandata, sRN LMDscandata still returns an sRA LMDscandata telegram, but every field is 0. There is no error code, so check the output format first when you only receive zeros.

picoScan100 example: Enable LMDscandata output over CoLa A and TCP, following the receive-and-subscribe steps above.

docs.title: Angle Reference
docs.text: LMDscandata uses the CoLa angle convention: 90° points straight ahead along the sensor X axis. Compact, MSGPACK, and the REST API use 0° for straight ahead. The same full scan of the picoScan100 therefore starts at -48° in LMDscandata and at -138° in Compact. Subtract 90° from an LMDscandata angle to compare it with Compact or MSGPACK data. The start angle and the angular step in the telegram are given in 1/10000°.

docs.title: Configure and Parse
docs.text:
• Configure the picoScan100 telegram content, such as the echoes and RSSI, with sWN LMDscandatacfg. Smaller telegrams reduce PLC load.
  • The picoScan100 field layout is in the picoScan100 CoLa Telegram Listing.
  • For TCP stream parsing (partial and concatenated telegrams), follow PLC Integration.

picoScan100 example: Read an LMDscandata telegram and understand its fields before implementing a parser.

docs.title: MSGPACK Format
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 picoScan100

MSGPACK encodes the measurement data with the MessagePack standard. Unlike Compact, it is self-describing: every field has a keyword, so any standard MessagePack library can parse it without knowing the exact layout. The price is more bandwidth than Compact.

Like Compact, each data package carries one scan segment. Each segment can be processed on its own for low latency; collect all segments with the same FrameNumber to get a complete scan. See multiScan100 segments and picoScan100 segments for device-specific behavior.

SICK's Python ScanSegmentAPI (scansegmentapi/msgpack.py) is the reference implementation of this format.

docs.title: Framing
docs.text:
Each MSGPACK buffer is wrapped in a frame. Size and checksum are little-endian uint32 values.

Framing: offset, size, and content.

Offset Size Content 0 4 bytes 02 02 02 02 (4 × <STX>) 4 4 bytes Size n of the MSGPACK buffer in bytes (without the checksum) 8 n bytes MSGPACK buffer 8 + n 4 bytes CRC32 over the MSGPACK buffer only, without the STX bytes and the size

docs.title: MSGPACK Keywords
docs.text:
To save bandwidth, keywords are encoded as uint8 codes instead of strings. Map the codes back to names with the table below. After removing the framing, parse the buffer with a standard MessagePack parser. Some parsers must be told to accept integer map keys; in Python:

unpacked = msgpack.unpackb(msgpack_buffer, strict_map_key=False)

docs.title: Used MSGPACK Keywords and Associated uint8 Codes
docs.text:
Names follow the SICK reference implementation. Some examples use different capitalization, such as TimeStampStart or PropertyValues; on the wire only the code is sent.

Used MSGPACK Keywords and Associated uint8 Codes: keyword name, code, and description.

Keyword name Code Description class 0x10 Class name of the map: Scan or ScanSegment (ScanSegment, Scan) data 0x11 Data part of a ScanSegment, Scan, or array (arrays) numOfElems 0x12 Number of elements in an array elemSz 0x13 Size of one array element in bytes endian 0x14 Endianness of the array elements elemTypes 0x15 Type of the array elements little 0x30 Value: little-endian float32 0x31 Value: data type float32 uint32 0x32 Value: data type uint32 uint8 0x33 Value: data type uint8 uint16 0x34 Value: data type uint16 int16 0x35 Value: data type int16 ChannelTheta 0x50 Channel with azimuth angles ChannelPhi 0x51 Channel with elevation angles DistValues 0x52 Channel with distance values RssiValues 0x53 Channel with RSSI values PropertiesValues 0x54 Channel with beam properties, for example reflector Scan 0x70 Class name Scan TimestampStart 0x71 Time stamp of the first beam of a scan TimestampStop 0x72 Time stamp of the last beam of a scan ThetaStart 0x73 Azimuth angle of the first beam of a scan ThetaStop 0x74 Azimuth angle of the last beam of a scan ScanNumber 0x75 Scan number ModuleID 0x76 ID of the measuring module BeamCount 0x77 Number of beams in a scan EchoCount 0x78 Number of echoes in a scan ScanSegment 0x90 Class name ScanSegment SegmentCounter 0x91 Segment number FrameNumber 0x92 Frame number Availability 0x93 Availability of a segment SenderId 0x94 Sender ID (device serial number) SegmentSize 0x95 Segment size SegmentData 0x96 Array with the measurement data per layer LayerId 0xA0 Array with layer IDs TelegramCounter 0xB0 Telegram counter TimestampTransmit 0xB1 Transmit time stamp

docs.title: Serialization of a Segment
docs.text:
Each data package carries one ScanSegment. Its SegmentData array holds one Scan per layer of the sensor:

ScanSegment
├── TelegramCounter
├── TimestampTransmit
├── SegmentCounter
├── FrameNumber
├── Availability
├── SenderId
├── LayerId
└── SegmentData
    ├── Scan 1
    ├── Scan 2
    ├── ...
    └── Scan N

Metadata fields are plain MessagePack values. Measurement arrays (distances, RSSI, angles, properties) are an exception: they are stored as binary blobs, see Serialization Of Arrays.

docs.title: Notation Used
docs.text:
The following notes on the notation used relate to the description of the structures encoded in MSGPACK:

  • msgpack_map_header denotes the header of a MessagePack map, see the MessagePack specification.
  • Names correspond to the keyword table; on the wire, each name is its uint8 code.
  • Angle brackets mark placeholders, for example <numOfElems> for the number of array elements.
  • The structures are written in a JSON-like notation, but the data is encoded according to the MessagePack specification.

docs.title: Serialization of the ScanSegment Class
docs.text:
The ScanSegment class is represented as a nesting of MSGPACK maps as follows:

msgpack_map_header {
  "class": ScanSegment,
  "data": msgpack_map_header {
    "TelegramCounter": <telegramCounter>,
    "TimestampTransmit": <timestampTransmit>,
    "SegmentCounter": <segmentCounter>,
    "FrameNumber": <frameNumber>,
    "Availability": <availability>,
    "SenderId": <senderId>,
    "LayerId": <layerIdVector>,
    "SegmentData": <segmentData>
  }
}

The meaning of the individual fields is shown in the following table.

Serialization of the ScanSegment Class: name, type, and description.

Name Type Description TelegramCounter MSGPACK int Counts all telegrams with measurement data sent in MSGPACK format since switching on the device. The counter starts at 1. TimestampTransmit MSGPACK int Sensor system time in µs since 1.1.1970 00:00 in UTC. SegmentCounter MSGPACK int Index of the segment within the frame. FrameNumber MSGPACK int Counts the number of full revolutions since the device was started. Availability MSGPACK int Reserved SenderId MSGPACK int Device serial number. It can be used to detect on the recipient which sensor the data was sent from. LayerId MSGPACK array of int Array of layer indices. The layer indices start at 1 and increase with decreasing elevation angle. SegmentData MSGPACK array of scans Array of elements of the Scan class (see Serialization Of The Scan Class) that contain the actual measurement data. The following applies: The scan at position i has the layer number LayerId[i].

The arrays LayerId and SegmentData are MSGPACK arrays as per the MSGPACK specification and are not represented like arrays containing measurement data (see "Serialization of arrays").

docs.title: Serialization of the Scan Class
docs.text:
The Scan class is represented as a nesting of MSGPACK maps as follows:

msgpack_map_header {
  "class": Scan,
  "data": msgpack_map_header {
    "TimestampStart": <timestampStart>,
    "TimestampStop": <timestampStop>,
    "ThetaStart": <thetaStart>,
    "ThetaStop": <thetaStop>,
    "ScanNumber": <scanNumber>,
    "ModuleID": <moduleId>,
    "ChannelTheta": <channelTheta>,
    "ChannelPhi": <channelPhi>,
    "DistValues": <distValues>,
    "RssiValues": <rssiValues>,
    "PropertiesValues": <propertiesValues>,
    "BeamCount": <beamCount>,
    "EchoCount": <echoCount>
  }
}

The meaning of the individual fields is shown in the following table:

Serialization of the Scan Class: name, type, and description.

Name Type Description TimestampStart MSGPACK int Acquisition time of the first beam of the scan in µs. The device's internal time base is used or, if the sensor offers the feature, the time set externally. TimestampStop MSGPACK int Acquisition time of the last beam of the scan in µs. The device's internal time base is used or, if the sensor offers the feature, the time set externally. ThetaStart MSGPACK int Azimuth angle of the first beam of the scan in radians. ThetaStop MSGPACK int Azimuth angle of the last beam of the scan in radians. ScanNumber MSGPACK int Not used. ModuleID MSGPACK int Number of the physical module that generated the data. In the case of the multiScan100, for example, this is one of the two measuring modules. ChannelTheta array of float32 Array of azimuth angles of a specific beam in radians. The encoding of the data in this array is described in "Serialization of arrays". The user can configure whether the array is present in the data structure. ChannelPhi array of float32 Array with the elevation angle of the scan in radians. Each Scan covers one layer, so this array contains one element. The encoding of the data in this array is described in "Serialization of arrays". The user can configure whether the array is present in the data structure. DistValues array of (array of float32) Array containing an array of distance values for each echo of the scan. The number of sub-arrays corresponds to the number of echoes in the scan, see also the EchoCount field below. The distance values are specified in mm. The encoding of the data in this array is described in "Serialization of arrays". The user can configure whether the array is present in the data structure. RssiValues array of (array of uint16) Array containing an array of RSSI values for each echo of the scan. The number of sub-arrays corresponds to the number of echoes in the scan, see also the EchoCount field below. For the representation of RSSI values, see RSSI scaling. The encoding of the data in this array is described in "Serialization of arrays". The user can configure whether the array is present in the data structure. PropertiesValues array of uint8 Array with additional properties, for example "reflector", for each beam of a scan. The encoding of the data in this array is described in "Serialization of arrays". This array is optional. BeamCount MSGPACK int Number of beams in the current scan. EchoCount MSGPACK int Number of echoes in the current scan.

For more details about the MSGPACK int format family, see the official msgpack specification.

DistValues and RssiValues array structure.

The diagram illustrates the nested array structure with 3 echoes and 15 beams, showing how each beam contains values for all echoes in both DistValues and RssiValues arrays.

docs.title: Serialization of Arrays
docs.text:
Arrays of measurement data (ChannelTheta, ChannelPhi, DistValues, RssiValues, and PropertiesValues) are encoded as follows:

msgpack_map_header {
  "numOfElems": <number of array elements>,
  "elemSz": <size of one array element in bytes>,
  "endian": little,
  "elemTypes": <typesArray>,
  "data": <binaryData>
}

The meaning of the individual fields of the Array class are shown in the following table.

Serialization of Arrays: name and description.

Name Description numOfElems Number of array elements elemSz Size of an array element in bytes, e.g., 4 for float32 or 1 for uint8. endian The value is always little elemTypes Array of element types. Only arrays with one element are supported here. Example: {float32} for an array of float32 values. An array of tuples would need multiple element types; such arrays are not used. data Actual payload. The data is encoded as a byte array in the MSGPACK format and can be copied directly into a structure/array after parsing the MSGPACK structure, taking into account the endianness and the data type.

docs.title: WebSocket Events
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan200 picoScan100

Instead of polling the REST API for state, you can open one persistent WebSocket connection, register the events you care about, and the device pushes a JSON frame every time a value changes. Use it for low-latency notifications: field-evaluation results, I/O switching, temperature alarms, firmware-update progress.

docs.title: Endpoint and Connection
docs.text:
ws://<device-ip>/apievents

Port 80 is used, and no authentication is required to open the connection. No periodic ping/keep-alive is needed. Every event has a matching REST endpoint of the same name; the data payload is identical to GET /api/<EventName>. Use REST for one-shot reads/writes, WebSocket for change notifications. See the multiScan200 and picoScan100 REST API references for the corresponding endpoint definitions. An event is available only where the device has the matching endpoint.

Compression depends on the device firmware. multiScan200 (firmware >1.1.0) and picoScan150 (firmware >2.3.3), the handshake does not negotiate permessage-deflate, and event registrations works with compression both enabled and disabled.

docs.title: Message Format
docs.text:
All messages are JSON text frames. Five types are used.

Register (client → device): one message per event, where clientId is a caller-chosen integer echoed back for that registration.

{ "type": "register", "event": "temperatureAlarmStatus", "clientId": 1 }

Registration confirmation (device → client): on success (status: 0) the device immediately sends the current value. Dispatch it exactly like a live event; it is your first data point.

{ "type": "register", "event": "temperatureAlarmStatus", "clientId": 1,
  "status": 0, "data": { "AlarmState": "NoAlarm" } }

Event push (device → client): sent whenever the value changes.

{ "type": "event", "event": "temperatureAlarmStatus", "clientId": 1,
  "status": 0, "data": { "AlarmState": "OverTemp" } }

Error (device → client): sent for an unknown or unavailable event. The connection stays open and other registrations are unaffected.

{ "type": "register", "event": "nonExistentEvent", "clientId": 2,
  "status": 1, "error": "Failed to register event ... Does the event exist?" }

Deregister (client → device): no response is sent.

{ "type": "deregister", "event": "temperatureAlarmStatus", "clientId": 1 }

docs.title: Step by Step
docs.text:
Send registration messages one at a time with at least 200 ms between consecutive frames. If several register frames arrive in a tight burst the device resets the connection. The delay is only needed during the initial registration sequence.

  1. Open the WebSocket to ws://<device-ip>/apievents; let the client negotiate any supported extensions.
  2. Register your events, one register per event, unique clientId, at least 200 ms apart.
  3. Receive initial values: each successful registration replies with type: "register", status: 0, and the current value in data. Dispatch it like a live event.
  4. Handle events: keep reading; on change the device pushes type: "event".
  5. Handle errors and reconnect: log any status != 0; other registrations still work.

docs.title: Python Example
docs.text:
This script uses the websockets library (pip install websockets), which negotiates supported extensions automatically. It registers two events 200 ms apart and dispatches the initial values and all later changes:

import asyncio
import json

import websockets

DEVICE_IP = "192.168.0.1"
EVENTS = ["CurrentTempDev", "DeviceStatus"]


async def main():
    async with websockets.connect(f"ws://{DEVICE_IP}/apievents", ping_interval=None) as ws:
        for client_id, event in enumerate(EVENTS, start=1):
            await ws.send(json.dumps({"type": "register", "event": event, "clientId": client_id}))
            await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
        async for message in ws:
            msg = json.loads(message)
            if msg.get("status", 0) != 0:
                print("Error:", msg["event"], msg.get("error"))
            elif msg["type"] in ("register", "event"):
                print(msg["event"], msg["data"])


asyncio.run(main())

Example code: MIT License, © 2026 SICK AG. Provided as is, without warranty. Test it before you use it with a machine or in production.

docs.title: Advanced: Throttle and Queue
docs.text:
Pass an optional options object when registering.

Throttle caps delivery frequency; excess events are dropped before queuing:

{ "type": "register", "event": "LSPdatetime", "clientId": 7,
  "options": { "throttle": { "minOutputIntervalMs": 5000 } } }

Queue means each event has its own per-event queue on the shared connection:

"options": { "queue": { "priority": "HIGH", "maxSize": 10, "discardIfFull": "OLDEST" } }

Advanced: Throttle and Queue: field, values, default, and meaning.

Field Values Default Meaning priority HIGH, MID, LOW MID Processing priority among events on this connection maxSize integer 1 Maximum buffered events discardIfFull OLDEST, NEWEST OLDEST Which event to drop when full

docs.title: Subscribable Events
docs.text:
Event names are case-sensitive. Full data schemas are in the OpenAPI spec under the matching GET endpoint.

Subscribable Events: event, typical trigger, and devices.

Event Typical trigger Devices DeviceStatus Device operational state changes multiScan200, picoScan100 SCdevicestate Safety controller state multiScan200, picoScan100 FieldEvaluationResult Object enters/leaves a detection field multiScan200, picoScan150 perpendicularDistanceResult Perpendicular-distance result changes picoScan150 OutputState / PortState Digital I/O state changes (PortState preferred) multiScan200, picoScan100 InputState Digital input state changes multiScan200, picoScan150 ContaminationData / ContaminationResult Lens contamination per sector / global result multiScan200, picoScan150 InertialMeasurementUnit Live IMU data multiScan200, picoScan150 CurrentTempDev Device temperature (°C) multiScan200, picoScan100 temperatureAlarmStatus Temperature alarm threshold crossed multiScan200 UpdateState Firmware-update progress multiScan200, picoScan100 LSPdatetime Device clock tick (every second) multiScan200, picoScan100

"picoScan100" means both the picoScan120 and the picoScan150. The message examples above use temperatureAlarmStatus; on the picoScan100, use CurrentTempDev instead.

docs.title: Test with Insomnia
docs.text:
Before wiring subscriptions into your app, verify them interactively in Insomnia:

  1. Create a WebSocket request to ws://<device-ip>/apievents and click Connect.
  2. Send one register message, for example { "type": "register", "event": "CurrentTempDev", "clientId": 1 }.
  3. Check the received messages: the registration reply with the current value comes first, then one event message per change.

picoScan100: WebSocket Event API.

docs.title: Reliability and Reconnect
docs.text: The device may close the connection on network interruption or firmware restart, and no subscription state is preserved across connections. On a close event, wait, reconnect, and re-register every subscription.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Troubleshooting: symptom, likely cause, and fix.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Connection refused Wrong IP / not reachable Ping the device; check firewall Resets after first registration Register frames sent too fast ≥ 200 ms between register messages Closes immediately (error 1002) Frame or extension negotiation mismatch Check Sec-WebSocket-Extensions and firmware; use a client compatible with the negotiated extensions "Event not found" Wrong name (case-sensitive) or absent on this firmware Check the exact name; confirm firmware No events after registration Value hasn't changed; events are change-driven Expected; the initial value is still sent on registration Stale app state at startup Dispatch filter only accepts type == "event" Also dispatch type == "register" with status == 0 Frequent drops Read timeout too short Set read timeout ≥ 300 s; events can be infrequent

Test subscriptions from a plain browser (Chrome/Edge) or from Insomnia/Postman before wiring them into your app. Wireshark on the sensor interface shows the raw WebSocket traffic.

docs.title: Device-Specific Guides
docs.text:
Choose your sensor family for wiring, web-interface walkthroughs, command references, downloads, and firmware information.

  • LRS4000: long-range 2D LiDAR, including motor synchronization.
  • multiScan100: multi-layer 3D LiDAR, including multiScan136, multiScan165, and multiScan166.
  • multiScan200: 3D LiDAR, including multiScan270.
  • picoScan100: compact 2D LiDAR, including picoScan120 and picoScan150.

docs.title: Integration Notes
docs.text:
Connect sensor data and configuration to your application using the tools and interfaces that fit your system.

  • 3D With 2D LiDARs: combine planar scans and motion information into point clouds.
  • Cable Dimensioning: estimate supply-cable voltage drop.
  • Coding Tools & Examples: find SDKs, clients, scan receivers, and parser definitions.
  • Cybersecurity: review network access, passwords, HTTPS, and data integrity.
  • Kaitai Struct Parsers: generate Compact parsers from format definitions.
  • MATLAB Integration: receive native ROS 2 point clouds with ROS Toolbox.
  • Milestones Camera Plugin: integrate cameras with Milestone XProtect and align timing.
  • Model Context: give coding assistants context from local documentation repositories.
  • PLC Integration: exchange CoLa B telegrams with PLCs over TCP.
  • ROS Integration: choose native ROS 2 or the host-side driver.

docs.title: 3D with 2D LiDARs
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 picoScan100

The LRS4000 and the picoScan100 measure distance and intensity in a single plane. Mounting the sensor on a motorized axis (tilt, rotation, or a linear stage) sweeps that plane through 3D space. If an incremental encoder is attached to the axis, the rotation angle at the moment of each scan is known precisely. This means every 2D point can be rotated into a common 3D frame, and a full sweep becomes a dense 3D point cloud.

Both approaches work on both devices. The ports below are examples; use the ports configured on your sensor. The LRS4000 sends Compact over TCP instead of UDP; see Compact Format: Transport.

Two approaches exist. Choose based on where you want the geometry code to run.

3D with 2D LiDARs: comparison criterion, Approach A (host-side), and Approach B (on-device).

Approach A (host-side) Approach B (on-device) Angle source Encoder wired to the sensor Encoder wired to the sensor, or the built-in IMU Processing Host receives the scan frames and applies the 3D transform Device accumulates and saves a PCD file internally Result One host-generated .pcd per sweep Single .pcd file stored on the device Best for Custom transforms, real-time streaming, maximum flexibility Simple integration, no host-side geometry code

For every scan frame, the sensor sends an encoder telegram (Compact type 4) with the same frame_number and the encoder tick count. This gives frame-accurate synchronization without timing jitter between the scan and position streams. Encoder input is available on the LRS4000 and the picoScan150.

docs.title: Hardware and Ports
docs.text:
A typical example is a sensor on a motorized tilt axis with a SICK DFS60-series incremental encoder wired to the sensor's encoder input. The same idea applies to rotation or linear stages: what matters is that an encoder on the moving axis feeds the sensor so each scan frame carries a position value.

Hardware and Ports: stream, protocol, port, and content.

Stream Protocol Port Content Scan data Compact UDP 2115 2D distance + intensity per segment, with frame_number Encoder data Compact UDP 7504 tick_count, reference ticks, speed, frame_number

Enable encoder data output (EncoderDataEnable, destination in EncoderDataEthSettings, default port 7504) and reset the encoder counter at the reference position before you collect data. The Configuration backup & restore flow is a convenient way to apply a validated encoder configuration.

docs.title: Synchronize by Frame Number
docs.text:
Both UDP streams carry a frame_number. Build a lookup table from that number to the encoder tick, so you can retrieve the exact axis angle for any scan frame even when the two streams arrive slightly out of order:

on encoder packet:  encoder_map[packet.frame_number] = packet.tick_count
on scan frame:      tick = encoder_map.lookup(frame.frame_number)  # or most-recent tick

Keep the table bounded in size to avoid unbounded memory growth over long acquisitions.

docs.title: Coordinate Transform
docs.text:
Convert each encoder tick to an angle, then rotate the 2D scan point around the axis. For a tilt axis along the world Y-axis with the scan plane horizontal at the reference:

theta   = (tick / ticks_per_revolution) * 2 * PI      # radians
x_world = x_scan * cos(theta)
y_world = y_scan                                       # lateral axis unchanged
z_world = x_scan * sin(theta)

Set ticks-per-revolution correctly. This value is specific to your encoder model. A mismatch produces a distorted point cloud. Reset the encoder counter at the reference position so tick 0 is your angular origin, and adapt the transform for a different axis orientation or a linear stage.

docs.title: End-to-End Pseudocode
docs.text:
Reset the encoder counter to establish tick 0:

POST /api/mResetEncoderIncrement

Process the two UDP streams and transform each scan frame. The udp_listen, run_until_interrupted, and save_pcd calls are placeholders for your UDP receiver, Compact parser, and PCD writer:

import math

TICKS_PER_REV = 10000     # set to your encoder's ticks per revolution
encoder_map = {}          # frame_number -> tick
last_tick = 0
cloud_pts = []

def on_encoder_packet(pkt):
    global last_tick
    encoder_map[pkt.frame_number] = pkt.tick_count
    last_tick = pkt.tick_count

def on_scan_frame(frame, points_2d):
    tick = encoder_map.pop(frame.frame_number, last_tick)
    theta = (tick / TICKS_PER_REV) * 2 * math.pi
    for x, y, intensity in points_2d:
        cloud_pts.append({
            "x": x * math.cos(theta),
            "y": y,
            "z": x * math.sin(theta),
            "intensity": intensity,
        })

udp_listen(port=2115, callback=on_scan_frame)       # placeholder
udp_listen(port=7504, callback=on_encoder_packet)   # placeholder
run_until_interrupted()                             # placeholder
save_pcd(cloud_pts, "cloud.pcd")                    # placeholder

Example code: MIT License, © 2026 SICK AG. Provided as is, without warranty. Test it before you use it with a machine or in production.

The sick_perception_sdk (C++17) is a good starting point for a host-side implementation.

docs.title: Approach B: On-Device Scan Merger
docs.text: The device combines the 2D scans with the IMU or encoder angle itself and stores one .pcd file. See 3D Scan Recording for the configuration and workflow.

docs.title: Cable Dimensioning
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Select a device to prefill its power consumption, minimum sensor voltage, and number of supply wires. Choose a load condition to check typical, maximum, or startup consumption where specified in the operating instructions. Custom Values lets you adjust the device-specific inputs, for example to add digital output loads or combine sensors. Supply voltage and cable specifications remain editable for every device. Select the question-mark icon beside an input for guidance.

Input

Device Load condition

Power consumption [W] ?

Typical or maximum power consumption from the technical data in the operating instructions. Include digital output loads and add all sensors sharing the cable.

Minimum sensor voltage [V] ?

Lower limit of the supply voltage range in the technical data of the operating instructions.

Supply voltage at the power supply [V] ?

Output voltage of the power supply under load, minus its tolerance. Typically 24 V.

Cable length [m] ?

One-way length from the power supply to the sensor connector, including extension cables.

Cross-section per wire [mm²] ?

Conductor cross-section from the cable data sheet, often given as AWG.

0.14 (AWG 26)0.25 (AWG 24)0.34 (AWG 22)0.5 (AWG 20)0.75 (AWG 18)1.0 (AWG 17)1.5 (AWG 16) Parallel wires per supply path ?

Number of wires connected in parallel for supply and for ground. See the pin assignment of the sensor connector.

12 Wire temperature [°C] ?

Highest expected temperature of the cable in operation. Warmer copper has a higher resistance.

Result

Voltage at the sensor– Minimum supply voltage– Margin– Voltage drop ΔU– Current I– Loop resistance R– Maximum cable length–

The curve shows the sensor voltage; dashed lines mark the voltage and length limits.

General remarks:

  • Measure the voltage at the sensor connector under load to verify the installation.
  • Check the startup load as well as normal operation: the starting current can cause a voltage drop that prevents the sensor from starting.
  • Take the supply voltage range and power consumption of your variant from its operating instructions on sick.com, and include digital output loads in the entered power.
  • To reduce voltage drop, shorten the cable, increase its cross-section, use two parallel wires per path (halves the resistance), or use a higher permitted supply voltage.
  • This estimate does not check cable ampacity, connector ratings, fusing, or electrical safety.

Device-specific remarks:

  • Device presets default to maximum operating consumption, not startup consumption. Select the startup load where available, or use Custom Values with the startup data from the operating instructions.
  • LRS4000 presets exclude digital output loads; select Custom Values to add them.
  • The multiScan100 presets cover multiScan136, multiScan165, and multiScan166; multiScan200 uses multiScan270 data; picoScan100 uses picoScan150 data. Verify the operating instructions for your exact variant.
  • multiScan270 requires both supply and ground pin pairs: see Electrical Connection.

Both supply and return wires contribute to voltage drop:

Cable resistance reduces the voltage at the sensor by ΔU.

docs.title: Cybersecurity
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Download the product-specific Cybersecurity Hardening Guide from Downloads on the individual product page at sick.com: LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, or picoScan100.

Cybersecurity covers the entire product life cycle. Increasing digitalization and network complexity in production plants increases the risk of cyberattacks from inside or outside the production network. A comprehensive cybersecurity strategy is therefore essential.

The asset owner is responsible for installing and maintaining security measures. Securing SICK devices in a network requires the active participation of the asset owner.

The recommendations below apply to the LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100. Menus, default states, available services, and authentication requirements vary by family, variant, and firmware. Sections with device-specific values name the products they cover. Confirm settings in the product-specific hardening guide and the device interface before applying them.

This page covers:

  • Communication security and access management
  • Application and field-evaluation aspects
  • User levels
  • Device interfaces
  • Ethernet-related settings

docs.title: Further Cybersecurity Information
docs.text:
For a cybersecurity overview, see SICK PSIRT. Current security advisories are listed on the SICK PSIRT Security Advisories page. Report security issues to the SICK Product Security Incident Response Team (SICK PSIRT). Read SICK's Information Handling Policies before sending security details.

Product-specific settings and telegram details are available from the device documentation. The product page is available through the SICK Product ID: pid.sick.com/{P/N}/{S/N}, where {P/N} is the part number and {S/N} is the serial number shown on the type label. The same part number links the device to its Asset Administration Shell, which holds the data sheet, operating instructions, certificates, and CAD data of the product type.

The examples and recommended settings on this page are general guidance, not customer-specific solutions or a replacement for specialist technical advice.

docs.title: Intended Use
docs.text:
These are non-contact LiDAR sensors for indoor or outdoor, mobile or stationary use in stand-alone operation. LRS4000 and picoScan100 are 2D LiDAR families; multiScan100 and multiScan200 are multi-layer 3D LiDAR families. Depending on the device, configuration, and application software, typical applications include:

  • Continuous output of measurement data
  • Monitoring freely defined fields, with object detection signaled through digital outputs or telegrams
  • Stationary field protection, area monitoring, and access control
  • Navigation and anti-collision for mobile platforms
  • Profile detection, collision protection, object protection, and access monitoring
  • 3D mapping, environment perception, and volume monitoring (multiScan200)

Use the device only in industrial environments (EN 61000-6-4). Incorrect use, improper modification, or tampering invalidates any warranty and may result in damage for which SICK AG accepts no responsibility.

docs.title: Environmental Influences
docs.text: For outdoor variants, fog, steam, dust, rain, and snow can affect the detection range. The effect can only be quantified through a verification test at the intended site.

docs.title: Restrict Physical Access
docs.text: Operate the device in a protected area where only instructed and approved personnel have access.

docs.title: Limit Exposure to Public Networks
docs.text: Do not use the devices in public networks. Use an isolated network wherever possible to reduce exposure and risk.

docs.title: Establish an Update Strategy
docs.text:
Keep the device firmware up to date:

  1. Search for the product at sick.com.
  2. Check Downloads for the latest firmware version and release notes.
  3. Check for updates regularly and apply them as they become available.
  4. Test updates in the specific installation before deploying them at larger scale.

Perform firmware updates only in a trusted environment. Release notes contain information about included security patches.

docs.title: Configuration Backup and Restore
docs.text: Keep a protected backup of a known-working configuration so that the device can be returned to a secure state. The Backup & restore workflow supports multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100. A passphrase can encrypt the backup. File-transfer authentication differs by firmware; follow the instructions for the matching OpenAPI file.

docs.title: Data Integrity
docs.text: Verify downloaded .spk and .sdd files with the instructions at sick.com/verify-downloads. The LFTchecksum workflow is available on multiScan200 and picoScan100.

docs.title: Brute-Force Protection
docs.text: After five consecutive unsuccessful login attempts, the picoScan100 enters a 30-second time lock. Other families can use a different threshold or lockout duration.

docs.title: Periodic Security Tests
docs.text: Regularly verify that the security system works as intended and document the results.

docs.title: Device Identification
docs.text:
Verify that the correct device type and system plug are connected. The product ID uniquely identifies the device and consists of its part number and serial number. Find the product ID on the device and system-plug labels, or read it through the user interface.

The device information also shows the currently installed firmware version, which follows semantic versioning. The device part number can also be read through the API:

GET http://192.168.0.1/api/OrderNumber

Read the serial number with GET http://192.168.0.1/api/SerialNumber. Together they form the product ID pid.sick.com/{P/N}/{S/N}. See Link A Device To Its AAS to connect this ID with the product type data.

For telegram-based access, refer to the CoLa / LMDscandata documentation and the Compact format.

docs.title: Use the Device-Not-Ready Status
docs.text: The Device-Not-Ready status signals that the device is not operating correctly. Monitor it through communication or a digital output. A change to this state while device parameters are being changed can be used as a manipulation warning.

docs.title: Protection Levels
docs.text:
Each protection level assumes that the recommendations from the previous level are followed.

Protection Levels: protection level, intended use, and procedures.

Protection level Use for Procedures No protection Demonstrations or test scenarios Set factory defaults Basic protection Recommended minimum for daily operation in an uncritical environment Check firmware and release notes; change all passwords; configure network settings; disconnect unused interfaces; close unused ports and services Advanced protection Exposed or critical systems with advanced security requirements Apply basic protection and limit network access by IP range

docs.title: No Protection
docs.text: In this state there are no access restrictions: passwords remain at their defaults and interfaces are active. Do not use this state for daily operation. Use it only for demonstrations or tests, or when physical access is restricted and the device is isolated from the network or protected by a firewall.

docs.title: Set Factory Defaults
docs.text:
To start from a known state:

  1. Log in to the device with user level Service.
  2. Verify the user level.
  3. Set the device to factory defaults.

The device resets default passwords and reboots with the standard IP address 192.168.0.1. If a different IP address was previously used, either open the default address in a web browser or search for and reconnect to the device in SOPAS ET.

docs.title: Basic Protection
docs.text: Basic protection is the minimum recommended level for daily operation in an uncritical environment.

docs.title: Check Firmware and Release Notes
docs.text: Critical vulnerabilities can be discovered during the device life cycle. Updating firmware is therefore an important cybersecurity measure. Before commissioning, install the latest firmware and review its release notes for security patches. Update only in a trusted environment.

docs.title: Change Passwords
docs.text:
Enable only the user levels required by the deployment and assign each a unique, secret password. Factory user-level states vary by family and firmware. Follow the User levels guide for the current activation and password workflow.

Use passwords containing uppercase letters, lowercase letters, special characters, and numbers. Change passwords over a confidential connection, preferably a point-to-point connection during initial commissioning.

docs.title: Reset the Service Password (picoScan100)
docs.text:
On picoScan100, only the Service password can be reset to its default through the password-reset process:

  1. Select Password forgotten.
  2. Send the generated email to the responsible SICK sales company or service partner listed at sick.com/worldwide.
  3. Paste the received code and select Reset.

Selecting Cancel aborts the process. Request a new reset code from the manufacturer if necessary.

To regain access to another user level, first reset the Service password, back up the configuration, and then reset the device to factory defaults.

docs.title: Configure Network Settings
docs.text:
The documented factory network defaults for the device families covered here are:

Configure Network Settings: setting and default.

Setting Default IP address 192.168.0.1 Subnet mask 255.255.255.0 Default gateway 0.0.0.0

The following factory defaults are documented for the multiScan270 (Operating Instructions 8031195/0000, issue 2026-09-30) and picoScan150 (Hardening Guide 8029481/1S7Z, 2025-04). They do not describe all service ports or data-output settings. Confirm the defaults for other variants and firmware versions on the device.

Ports and service availability vary by device and firmware. The entries below identify the exact device variant documented; they are not family-wide defaults.
