docs.title: ScanSegmentAPI | JSON
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 picoScan100

Compact or MSGPACK data can be received with ScanSegmentAPI and stored as JSON. The Python ScanSegmentAPI supports LRS4000, multiScan100, and picoScan100; MSGPACK is available where the selected device supports that format. Use this workflow to create portable recordings for analysis, testing, and replay without requiring the sensor to remain connected.

Install the project with Poetry and run the JSON example:

git clone https://github.com/SICKAG/ScanSegmentAPI.git
cd ScanSegmentAPI
poetry install
poetry run python examples/store_segments_json_compact.py

Before you run it, set IP, PORT, and TRANSPORT_PROTOCOL at the top of the script. For UDP, IP is the receiving computer; for TCP, it is the sensor. The script stores 200 segments in segments.json. For MSGPACK, use store_segments_json_msgpack.py. See Using the ScanSegmentAPI from Python in the README for the API.

picoScan100 example: Record measurement data as JSON with ScanSegmentAPI for offline analysis and replay.

docs.title: sick_perception_sdk
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The sick_perception_sdk is mainly a C++17 SDK for receiving SICK LiDAR data and configuring sensors. It is listed under Recording because it converts received scans to PCD files, which you can store and open in tools such as CloudCompare. It provides event-driven, thread-safe data acquisition from multiple sensors and ready-to-use examples.

sick_perception_sdk data streaming, REST-based configuration, and additional tools.

docs.title: Supported Devices and Platforms
docs.text:
The SDK supports these device variants:

Supported Devices and Platforms: product family and variants.

Product family Variants LRS4000 LRS4581 multiScan100 multiScan136, multiScan165, multiScan166 multiScan200 multiScan270 picoScan100 picoScan120, picoScan150

The SDK's example build option targets LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, or picoScan100.

The project builds with CMake on Linux and Windows and supports x86_64 and ARM64. Tested platforms are Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, and Windows 11. macOS is not a tested platform.

docs.title: Build and Integrate
docs.text: The SDK uses CMake and Conan 2 is available for dependency management. Follow the upstream build instructions and CMake integration example for the current options and dependencies. The example build can be selected for a device family, and the CMake project exposes separate components for drivers, sensor configuration, and Compact format.

docs.title: Receive and Record Data
docs.text:
The SDK receives event-driven scan, IMU, and encoder data using SICK's Compact format over TCP or UDP. Scan data is exposed as point clouds (Public PointField::DataType API).

The Compact-format layer provides a PointCloudToPCDConverter helper for converting scan-derived point clouds to PCD. There is ready-made recording application; you can use it to write the PCD files from your own code. The sensor_configuration component provides REST-based access to sensor settings and status.

docs.title: Threading, Diagnostics, and Logging
docs.text:
Data acquisition is thread-safe and event-driven, including when acquiring from multiple sensors. The SDK includes diagnostic examples and built-in diagnostic and logging capabilities. The default logger uses plog; applications can provide a custom logger and set a minimum log level.

See the SDK README for current setup details, examples, and API documentation.

docs.title: SOPASair Recorder | .sc
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 picoScan100

The SOPASair Data recorder saves real LiDAR measurement scenarios as .sc files for later analysis and replay.

docs.title: Open the Data Recorder
docs.text:
In the sensor's SOPASair web interface, open Diagnostics → Data recorder. The page provides an installation file for a separate recorder application:

  1. Download the data recorder installation file from SOPASair.
  2. Unzip the downloaded ZIP file and start the recorder application.
  3. In the Connection Wizard, connect the recorder to the device. The recorder interface opens in a new window.
  4. Use the recorder application to capture the measurement scenario and save the .sc recording for later use.

The recorder runs on Windows and Linux. To replay a recording, connect the recorder to the device and open the .sc file; the device plays back the recorded data internally.

The picoScan100 SOPASair Data recorder page links to the separate recorder application.

picoScan100 example: Record and replay a measurement scenario as an `.sc` file with SOPASair. Menu labels and recorder availability may differ by software version.

docs.title: When to Use It
docs.text:
• Capture a real scene during operation to investigate an intermittent issue.
  • Replay a captured measurement scenario to compare processing results across application changes, rather than returning to the installation site.
  • Share a recording with colleagues or SICK support for reproducible analysis.

Recordings capture a particular measurement scenario, not an entire device configuration or raw Ethernet traffic. Save the relevant configuration and firmware details separately when comparing behavior after changes. For a complete device configuration, use Backup & Restore; for raw network traffic, use Wireshark | pcap.

This is the SOPASair Data recorder workflow, not the separate legacy SOPAS ET Excel/CSV recording workflow. The availability of the recorder and replay functions may depend on device and software version; the illustrated entry point is from picoScan100. LRS4000 and multiScan100 also provide the SOPASair Diagnostics → Data recorder entry.

docs.title: Wireshark | pcap
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Packet captures record the raw Ethernet communication between the sensor and a host computer, for protocol-level diagnostics, network troubleshooting, decoder development, and SICK support. Capture with Wireshark, tcpdump, or tshark and save as .pcap or .pcapng.

To decode Compact captures, install the Wireshark Compact dissector.

Wireshark displaying decoded Compact measurement data with the SICK dissector.

picoScan100 example: Use the Wireshark dissector to decode Compact packets into readable fields when checking a capture before debugging your own decoder.

docs.title: Shared Features
docs.text:
Find cross-device setup and maintenance workflows here. Supported parameters and procedures vary by family; check the compatibility labels on each page.

  • Asset Administration Shell: access structured product data.
  • Checksums: compare firmware, calibration, and persisted-parameter digests.
  • Device State: inspect availability through LEDs, outputs, or device interfaces.
  • Device Discovery: find sensors on the local network.
  • Factory Reset: compare factory and application reset scopes and recovery steps.
  • Firmware Update: install matching firmware through supported tools or APIs.
  • IP Address Assignment: change network addresses and review IP change policies.
  • LiDAR License Activation: activate, inspect, or deactivate feature licenses.
  • Time Synchronization: align sensor clocks using NTP or PTP.
  • UDP Unicast / Multicast: choose and configure a measurement-data transport.
  • User Levels: manage authentication, access levels, and password recovery.

docs.title: Asset Administration Shell
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The Asset Administration Shell (AAS) is the standardized digital twin of Industry 4.0. SICK publishes an AAS for each product part number at aas.sick.com. Access requires a SICK ID login. The AAS describes the product type in a machine-readable format, which makes it useful for engineering tools and asset management systems.

docs.title: What to Expect
docs.text:
• Nameplate: manufacturer, product designation, order code, and markings such as CE and UKCA
  • Technical data: product classification (ECLASS, ETIM) and key technical properties
  • Documents: data sheet, operating instructions, dimensional drawing, and certificates
  • CAD data: 3D models such as STEP files and the EPLAN macro
  • Contact information: SICK sales and service contacts

The AAS describes the part number, not an individual device. Serial number, firmware version, configuration, status, and measurement data come from the device itself through the REST API, the CoLa interface, and the data streams.

docs.title: Link a Device to Its AAS
docs.text: Each device is identified by its product ID pid.sick.com/{P/N}/{S/N}, made of the part number and the serial number from the type label. Both values can also be read from the device over the REST API. The part number connects the device to its AAS.

docs.title: Checksums
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan200 picoScan100

The LFTchecksum is a read-only REST resource that returns MD5 digests over four independent software and configuration areas of the device. It lets you verify at any time that nothing has changed since a known-good reference: detect unintended parameter changes, confirm a configuration file applied correctly, or check that a firmware update touched only the areas it should.

See the multiScan200 or picoScan100 REST API reference for the endpoint definition.

docs.title: Reading It
docs.text:
No authentication required:

GET /api/LFTchecksum

{
  "header": { "status": 0, "message": "Ok" },
  "data": { "LFTchecksum": {
    "MD5SumOK":       true,
    "MD5LinuxRoot":   "8439a3f5bb209f3d51557d509169ec60",
    "MD5App":         "304f9a18302e2b635da2c2c220463119",
    "MD5Calibration": "bc5e5d5df638dc45c85937c8c67b59d7",
    "MD5Parameters":  "07f18c8032e24ac65ca0ed7c04be6a62"
  } }
}

docs.title: The Four Sub-Checksums
docs.text:
The Four Sub-Checksums: field, covers, and changes when….

Field Covers Changes when… MD5LinuxRoot Linux root filesystem (OS layer) A firmware update modifies the OS partition MD5App Application binary and libraries A firmware update installs a new application version MD5Calibration Factory calibration data Calibration is recalculated/overwritten (factory service only) MD5Parameters Persistent parameter set (EEPROM) Parameters are persisted via WriteEeprom, or a config file is imported and persisted MD5SumOK Overall integrity flag false if any of the four fails its internal verification

docs.title: RAM vs. Persistent Storage
docs.text:
The device keeps two parameter states at once:

RAM vs. Persistent Storage: parameter state, storage location, persistence after reboot, and effect on MD5Parameters.

State Where Survives reboot? Reflected in MD5Parameters? Working copy RAM No (a RebootDevice flushes RAM to EEPROM first, so it survives a software reboot) No, until WriteEeprom or RebootDevice Persisted copy EEPROM / flash Yes Yes

An unchanged MD5Parameters does not mean RAM is unchanged: REST writes modify the working copy. Unlike RebootDevice, which persists RAM first, SoftReset and a hard power-cycle discard unsaved changes.

docs.title: When Does Each Sub-Checksum Change?
docs.text:
The following table shows the behavior of a picoScan150 (● = changed, - = unchanged):

When Does Each Sub-Checksum Change? Scenario and resulting change of the LinuxRoot, app, calibration, and parameters checksums.

Scenario LinuxRoot App Calibration Parameters Two consecutive reads, no operation - - - - Change a parameter in RAM only (no WriteEeprom) - - - - Change in RAM, then SoftReset - - - - Change in RAM, then RebootDevice (persists first) - - - ● Change + WriteEeprom - - - ● CreateParameterBackup → RestoreParameterBackup, same file, no content change - - - - LoadApplicationDefaults (destructive) - - - ● Firmware upgrade ● ● - - Firmware downgrade ● ● - -

MD5Calibration does not change through normal end-user operations. A change there indicates a factory calibration update or an unexpected write to the calibration partition, so treat it as a red flag.

docs.title: A Practical Integrity Workflow
docs.text:
1. Record all four hashes from a known-good device (the reference).
  2. After any change (a config push, a restore, a firmware update), read LFTchecksum again.
  3. Compare field by field: a firmware update should move MD5LinuxRoot + MD5App only; a persisted config change should move MD5Parameters only; MD5Calibration should never move.
  4. Anything else is unexpected: investigate before putting the device back into service.

Compact and MSGPACK telegrams carry a CRC32 per packet (see Compact Format); CoLa B telegrams carry a 1-byte XOR checksum. The LFTchecksum covers the stored software and configuration, which complements these on-the-wire checks.

docs.title: Device Discovery
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

There are three ways to find a sensor:

  1. Use the default IP for a direct first connection.
  2. Use SOPAS ET network search when the sensor is already connected to a local network.
  3. Implement discovery yourself when discovery must be part of an application or provisioning workflow.

docs.title: Default IP
docs.text:
For a direct first connection, connect the sensor to the computer with Ethernet and use the factory default IP address:

Default IP: parameter and value.

Parameter Value Sensor IP address 192.168.0.1 Subnet mask 255.255.255.0

Set the computer's Ethernet adapter to a different address in the same subnet, for example 192.168.0.100, then open http://192.168.0.1/ in a browser. See Getting started for the Windows procedure.

docs.title: SOPAS ET Network Search
docs.text:
SOPAS ET provides a graphical network search for SICK devices. Connect the sensor to the same Ethernet segment as the computer and start the search. The result lists responsive devices with their IP address, MAC address, and device identity.

SOPAS ET network search showing a discovered picoScan device.

Use this approach when the sensor is already connected to a switch or when its configured address is unknown. The search uses the same local broadcast principle as the protocol described below; it does not cross routers. Whether the search finds the sensor and can change its IP address depends on the IP change policy.

docs.title: Your Own Implementation
docs.text:
SICK devices answer a UDP broadcast discovery telegram, so a host on the same segment can locate every device without knowing its address in advance. This requires no authentication and no REST call: send one broadcast datagram to 255.255.255.255:30718; every responsive device replies by unicast with its full network configuration.

This is a limited broadcast: it travels only within the local segment and is discarded at every router boundary. If the device is on a different subnet, connect a host to the same segment and set the address explicitly.

picoScan100 example: Discover devices on the network with Python before implementing the broadcast telegram workflow below. The sensor's SICK discovery service must be enabled.

docs.title: Request Telegram (24 Bytes)
docs.text:
Each field is at a fixed position:

Request Telegram (24 Bytes): bytes, field, value / source, and description.

Bytes Field Value / source Description 0 CMD 0x10 Command identifier for a scan (discovery) request 1 isBC 0x00 Unicast/broadcast origin flag, set 0x00 even when broadcasting 2-3 Length 0x00 0x08 Payload length, big-endian; always 8 for discovery 4-9 Host MAC FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF Sender MAC; all-ones for a broadcast request 10-13 Request ID random 4 bytes Fresh random per telegram; devices echo it so you can match replies 14 Scan flag 0x01 Marks a scan request; the device ignores the telegram if this isn't 0x01 15 Reserved 0x00 Must be zero 16-19 Interface IP host address Host interface IPv4, one byte per octet (big-endian) 20-23 Subnet mask host mask Host subnet mask, one byte per octet (big-endian)

docs.title: Python Example
docs.text:
This script sends the request telegram from the table above and prints every device that replies within 5 seconds. Set INTERFACE_IP and SUBNET_MASK to the adapter on the sensor subnet.

import os
import socket

INTERFACE_IP = "192.168.0.100"
SUBNET_MASK = "255.255.255.0"
TAGS = {b"EIPa": ("IP", 4), b"ENMa": ("Mask", 4), b"EDGa": ("Gateway", 4),
        b"EDhc": ("DHCP", 1), b"EMAC": ("MAC", 6)}


def field(data, tag, size):
    index = data.find(tag)  # value starts after the 4-byte tag and a 2-byte header
    return None if index < 0 else data[index + 6 : index + 6 + size]


def show(value):
    if len(value) == 4:
        return socket.inet_ntoa(value)
    return value.hex(":") if len(value) == 6 else ("DHCP" if value[0] else "static")


telegram = (bytes([0x10, 0x00, 0x00, 0x08]) + b"\xff" * 6 + os.urandom(4) + bytes([0x01, 0x00])
            + socket.inet_aton(INTERFACE_IP) + socket.inet_aton(SUBNET_MASK))

with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM) as sock:
    sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_BROADCAST, 1)
    sock.settimeout(5)
    sock.bind((INTERFACE_IP, 0))
    sock.sendto(telegram, ("255.255.255.255", 30718))
    seen = set()
    while True:  # collect every reply until the timeout
        try:
            data, sender = sock.recvfrom(1024)
        except socket.timeout:
            break
        values = {name: field(data, tag, size) for tag, (name, size) in TAGS.items()}
        identity = (sender[0], values.get("MAC"))
        if identity in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(identity)
        print(sender[0], {name: show(v) for name, v in values.items() if v})

Example code: MIT License, © 2026 SICK AG. Provided as is, without warranty. Test it before you use it with a machine or in production.

docs.title: Reply Fields
docs.text:
Each reply is a variable-length packet whose configuration fields are tagged: a 4-byte ASCII tag, a 2-byte internal header, then the field bytes. If a tag isn't found, that field isn't present in the response.

Parsing the Replies: tag, field, size, and encoding.

Tag Field Size Encoding EIPa Device IP address 4 IPv4 big-endian ENMa Subnet mask 4 IPv4 big-endian EDGa Default gateway 4 IPv4 big-endian EDhc DHCP flag 1 0x01 = DHCP, 0x00 = static EMAC MAC address 6 hex bytes, MSB-first

If a tag isn't found, that field isn't present in the response.

docs.title: Platform Notes
docs.text:
Set SO_BROADCAST before sending, or the send fails. On a multi-homed host, bind the socket to the IP of the adapter on the device subnet so the broadcast leaves the correct network interface card. On Windows, set the sensor network profile to Private; a Public profile blocks the inbound unicast replies. See Getting Started.

SICK's discovery tools perform the same broadcast with a GUI. Use them for a quick look; use the raw telegram above when you need discovery built into your own application or a headless provisioning script.

docs.title: Alternative When SICK Discovery Is Disabled: ARP
docs.text: On picoScan100, SICK's UDP discovery can be disabled for cybersecurity reasons. In that case, the sensor does not respond to the usual SOPAS ET or AppManager search. It can still announce its IP address using Gratuitous ARP, which lets you identify it without the SICK discovery broadcast. This approach finds devices visible on the local network; it does not replace the SICK protocol for discovering and retrieving full network configuration.

docs.title: Identify the Sensor in Wireshark
docs.text:
1. Connect the sensor directly to the computer or to a local network switch.
  2. Capture traffic on the Ethernet adapter connected to that network.
  3. Apply the display filter arp.
  4. Look for a SICK MAC address beginning with 00:06:77.
  5. Read the sensor IP address from the ARP packet details, then connect to that address.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Open an elevated Command Prompt and run:

arp -a

Find an entry whose MAC address begins with 00-06-77; the associated address is the sensor's IP. This only works when the sensor IP is within the computer's current subnet. To look beyond the default subnet, configure the network adapter with a wider subnet mask, such as 255.0.0.0.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Connect the sensor over Ethernet and run:

arp -n

Find a MAC address beginning with 00:06:77 and use its associated IP address. As on Windows, this only works when the sensor address is within the current subnet. A wider mask such as 255.0.0.0 can be used to reach devices outside the default subnet; 0.0.0.0 is not a valid subnet mask.

docs.title: Device State
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The sensors provide several ways to check whether they are available and ready to measure. Choose the local indication that suits the installation, or read the state through REST or CoLa from a host application.

docs.title: Status LEDs
docs.text: Status LEDs indicate the device state. On devices where the LEDs can be switched off, they do not indicate anything while disabled. See the device operating instructions for the meanings of the individual LED states.

docs.title: Digital Output: Device Not Ready
docs.text:
Use a digital output when an external controller or PLC needs a hardware signal for device availability:

  1. Open the sensor web interface and log in as Service.
  2. Open Inputs and Outputs.
  3. Select Device not ready as the source for the output that should signal the status.
  4. Configure the restart time, switching logic, and electrical connection logic for the installation.

If contamination is expected and should be signaled separately, select Contamination indication as an output source. See Contamination Indication for its configuration and behavior.

docs.title: Read State over REST or CoLa
docs.text:
Two state values are available. SCdevicestate gives a simple readiness result; DeviceStatus (REST) / DevSta (CoLa A/B) provides more detail:

Simple readiness (SCdevicestate): value and meaning.

Value Meaning 0 Busy or logged in 1 Ready 2 Error

Detailed state (DeviceStatus / DevSta): value and meaning.

Value State Meaning 0 Reserved Reserved value. 1 Startup The device is starting. 2 Service mode A service action is in progress, such as a software update or comprehensive parameter exchange. This state does not indicate whether the device can operate normally. 3 Normal operation Startup is complete and no errors or warnings have occurred. 4 Suspended operation An internal or environmental condition prevents adequate measurement. 5 Service recommended Measurement is operating as specified, but a service technician may need to address an issue. 6 Service required Measured values are still available, but the issue may affect them; service is required. 7 Recoverable error The device has a malfunction and measurement service is likely disrupted; service may be able to resolve it. 8 Fatal error A fatal error has occurred; reset and reboot the device.

For exact request and response formats, see the REST API references and the CoLa listing sections:

References: device, REST, DevSta, and SCdevicestate.

Device REST DevSta SCdevicestate LRS4000 OpenAPI – sRN SCdevicestate multiScan100 OpenAPI sRN DevSta sRN SCdevicestate multiScan200 OpenAPI sRN DevSta sRN SCdevicestate picoScan100 OpenAPI sRN DevSta, sEN DevSta sRN SCdevicestate, sEN SCdevicestate

docs.title: Factory Reset
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Use a factory reset to restore default device parameters, or an application reset to restore application settings while keeping communication settings. The key difference is whether the communication interfaces are reset.

docs.title: Choose the Reset Scope
docs.text:
Reset options: effect on settings and the corresponding SOPASair menu entries.

Action Effect SOPASair menu entry Factory reset Restores default parameters, including communication settings. The current connection can be lost. Reset to factory settings Application reset Resets application settings while retaining communication settings, such as the IP configuration. Reset and maintain communication interfaces

After a factory reset, the sensor IP address is 192.168.0.1 for LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100. An application reset keeps the current IP configuration.

docs.title: Before You Reset
docs.text:
1. Download a configuration backup and keep any required passphrase safe.
  2. Record the current IP configuration and check the device's default address so that you can reconnect after a factory reset.
  3. Ensure that resetting the configuration will not disrupt production or a safety-related process.

docs.title: Device Web Interface
docs.text:
Log in at the Service user level. Open the three-dot menu, select Device, choose the required reset option, and confirm it. Menu labels and availability can vary with firmware.

SOPASair Device menu: application reset retains communication interfaces; factory reset also restores their defaults.

docs.title: REST API or CoLa A/B
docs.text:
Reset methods: authenticated REST calls and CoLa method telegrams.

Action REST method CoLa A/B method Factory reset POST /api/LoadFactoryDefaults sMN mSCloadfacdef Application reset POST /api/LoadApplicationDefaults sMN mSCloadappdef

Choose one method, not both in sequence. Follow the REST authentication guide and the device's REST reference for LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, or picoScan120/150. For CoLa access levels and framing, see the LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, or picoScan120/150 telegram listings.

A reset changes parameters, not firmware. Reboot device (SoftReset) or a power cycle restarts the device without restoring factory defaults; unsaved changes can be lost.

docs.title: Firmware Update
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Update the firmware to get fixes and new functions. The available methods depend on the device:

  • LRS4000: Sentio Creator or SOPAS ET.
  • multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100: SOPASair, Sentio Creator, SOPAS ET, or the REST API.

docs.title: Where to Get the Package
docs.text:
Download the package that matches your device and target version from its product page under Downloads / Software: picoScan100, multiScan100, multiScan200, or LRS4000.

Sentio Creator can also provide firmware packages.

Read the release notes for your device before you update: LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, or picoScan100.

docs.title: Web GUI
docs.text:
Open the device's firmware page in SOPASair and follow the update workflow.

Firmware update in the Web GUI.

docs.title: SOPAS ET
docs.text:
1. Unpack the firmware package (.spk). Connect the sensor over Ethernet and keep the power supply stable during the update.
  2. Find the sensor in SOPAS ET, add it to the project, and save the parameter file (.sopas) as a precaution.
  3. Open the device settings, choose Download firmware, select the .spk package, and log in at the Service user level when prompted.
  4. Wait until the device has rebooted and its LED is green. Check the firmware version; reinstall the device driver if SOPAS ET asks for it.
  5. Check that the device works as expected. If its state is unclear, load the factory defaults at the Service user level and then load the saved parameter file.

docs.title: Sentio Creator
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Use Sentio Creator to discover the device, select the firmware version, and install the update.

Firmware update in Sentio Creator.

docs.title: Headless via the REST API
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Device-specific endpoints: multiScan100 REST API, multiScan200 REST API, and picoScan100 REST API.

Automate the update with the five steps below. Run them in order; skipping or reordering steps can leave the device in an inconsistent state. After flashing, the device reboots automatically and is unreachable for a few minutes. The update is successful only when the device is back online with the expected version.

docs.title: Get a Session Token
docs.text:
multiScan200 and picoScan100 use POST /api/CreateSessionToken at Service level with challenge-response. This endpoint also accepts HTTP Basic authentication, which is convenient in scripts:

POST /api/CreateSessionToken
Authorization: Basic <base64(Service:<password>)>
Content-Type: application/json

{}

Basic authentication sends the password only Base64-encoded. Use it only over HTTPS or on an isolated network.

The response contains the session token:

{ "header": { "status": 0 }, "data": { "token": "eyJhbGci..." } }

The multiScan100 REST interface documents /update, RunFirmwareUpdate, and UpdateState, but not CreateSessionToken. Use the authentication flow from the release notes or the OpenAPI file for the installed firmware.

docs.title: Upload the Package
docs.text:
PUT /api/update with the firmware file as the binary body. On multiScan200 and picoScan100, the X-Session-Token header authorizes this transfer, so Basic Auth is not required here.

PUT /api/update
X-Session-Token: <token>
Content-Type: application/octet-stream

<binary firmware file content>

A 200 OK confirms the package was received.

docs.title: Start the Update
docs.text:
POST /api/RunFirmwareUpdate accepts only challenge-response for POST:RunFirmwareUpdate, not Basic Auth or the session token:

{
  "header": {
    "nonce": "...",
    "opaque": "...",
    "realm": "...",
    "user": "Service",
    "response": "<computed hash>"
  }
}

docs.title: Poll the Update State
docs.text:
GET /api/UpdateState every ~5 s until it reaches Finished (2) or the device becomes unreachable (reboot started). Stop on Error (3) and investigate before retrying.

GET /api/UpdateState

Example response:

{ "data": { "UpdateState": 1 } }

docs.title: Verify the New Version
docs.text:
After the device is back online, read the identity and compare against the expected version:

GET /api/DeviceIdent

Example response:

{ "data": { "DeviceIdent": { "Name": "picoScan", "Version": "2.3.3.0R" } } }

DeviceIdent.Version and GET /api/FirmwareVersion may format the same firmware version slightly differently, so normalize them before comparing.

docs.title: UpdateState Values
docs.text:
UpdateState Values: value, state, and meaning.

Value State Meaning 0 Initial No update in progress. Package may be uploaded but flashing hasn't started. 1 Started Flashing in progress. Do not power-cycle the device. 2 Finished Flash complete; the device reboots automatically. 3 Error Update failed. Check package compatibility and retry. Do not power-cycle immediately.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
• PUT /api/update returns 403: Missing or expired session token. Create a fresh token and add X-Session-Token.
  • RunFirmwareUpdate returns header.status 4 (Access Denied) or 10 (Invalid Challenge): Basic Auth or the session token was used instead of challenge-response, or the challenge was invalidated. Use a new challenge for POST:RunFirmwareUpdate.
  • UpdateState = 3 (Error): Wrong package or an unsigned package on firmware V2.2.0 or later. Download the correct .spk.signed and retry.
  • Device never returns: Normal reboot takes 2-5 minutes. Wait and keep UDP sockets open across the reboot.

While UpdateState is Started (1), never power-cycle the device. Allow 2-5 minutes total for the flash and reboot. Keep measurement sockets open across the reboot, so the OS doesn't buffer an ICMP port-unreachable message that would break the first recv() call afterwards (on Windows, apply SIO_UDP_CONNRESET).

On multiScan200 and picoScan100, subscribe to the UpdateState WebSocket event instead of polling to get progress pushes during the flash. On multiScan200 and picoScan100, verify integrity after the update with the LFTchecksum: a firmware change updates MD5LinuxRoot and MD5App but leaves MD5Parameters and MD5Calibration untouched.

docs.title: Related Articles
docs.text:
How to perform a firmware update via HTTP.

How to perform a firmware update with SOPASair.

How to perform a firmware update with SOPAS ET.

docs.title: IP Address Assignment
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Changing the IP address through the SOPAS ET device search without login is restricted by an IP change policy. With the default policy, an IP change without login is only possible within the first 60 seconds after boot. After that, a user role with the required rights is needed, or the policy blocks the change entirely.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: Since firmware V2.1.0, the picoScan100 stores an IP change policy on the device instead of allowing unauthenticated IP changes; see the picoScan100 release notes.

docs.title: Policy Options
docs.text:
IP change policy: web UI option, behavior, and CoLa EtherCoLaScanMode value.

Option Behavior CoLa value Off The device cannot be found with the SOPAS ET broadcast search, and the IP address cannot be changed through it. 2 Change IP address without logging in IP change allowed without login. No time window. 0 Change IP address only when logged in Device visible in scans. IP change only with login. 1 Change IP address up to 1 min after start without logging in IP change allowed without login only in the first 60 s after boot. After that, login is required. Default setting on picoScan100. 3

The default can differ between device families and firmware versions; for example, device search is enabled by default on multiScan200. Read the active setting from the device before relying on it.

docs.title: Change the Policy (via Web UI)
docs.text:
1. Power on the device.
  2. Open the device IP address in a browser and log in.
  3. Go to Diagnostics > Cybersecurity > Services and protocols.
  4. Select one of the four options.
  5. Save and restart.

The policy is also available through EtherCoLaScanMode in the CoLa interface. See Set/Read Device Search Mode for multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100, and the EtherCoLaScanMode variable in the REST API references for multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100. The IP address itself is set with EIIpAddr, for example picoScan100 Set IP Address.

For a visual example of changing the address itself rather than the search policy, watch the picoScan100 example video in Getting Started.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• 60 s window expired: Reboot the device, or log in with credentials.
  • Device not in search: The policy Off may be active. Connect to the known IP address, or find it as described in Device Discovery.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
• Can I extend the 60 s window? No. After 60 s, a login is required.
  • Which user level is required? No login is required within the 60 s window. Outside it, see User Levels.
  • Should I downgrade the firmware? Not recommended. It reduces security.

docs.title: LiDAR License Management
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Some device functions require a license. Use the device's license manager to transfer an issued license code to the device. The exact screens and available options can vary by device and firmware.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
• Obtain a valid license code for the device. The code is formatted as five groups separated by hyphens.
  • Connect to the device and open its web interface.

docs.title: Activate a License
docs.text:
1. In a browser, connect to the device at http://<device-IP-address>/. On the device overview, choose View licenses.

Open the license overview from the device home page.

  1. In the license overview, choose Activate license.

The license overview also provides the action to deactivate returnable licenses.

  1. Select whether the device has an internet connection for the transfer, then choose Next.

Choose the transfer route that matches the device's network access.

  1. Enter or copy the license code. If the license ticket contains several entries, select the license entries to transfer, then continue.

Select the entries that should be transferred to the device.

  1. When the transfer succeeds, close the confirmation and check the updated license overview.

  2. Reboot the device.

docs.title: Deactivate or Return a License
docs.text: In the license overview, choose Deactivate license. During license selection, enter the license code for the license to deactivate, choose a license marked as returnable, then continue and confirm.

docs.title: Time Synchronization
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Synchronize sensor clocks with NTP or PTP to align measurements from multiple sensors and correlate scans with logs and external system events.

docs.title: NTP Time Synchronization
docs.text:
NTP uses a network time server; the sensor acts as a client.

picoScan100 example: Locate and configure the device-time settings before following the NTP setup below. Menu labels may differ with firmware.

docs.title: Offline NTP Server for picoScan100
docs.text:
The following describes configuring an Ubuntu host as a local NTP server and a picoScan100 as its client. This is useful when there is no Internet connection: the controller and sensor use a shared local time source.

Requirements:

  • An Ubuntu host connected to the sensor network. Ubuntu 24.04 no longer ships the ntp package; use chrony or ntpsec.
  • A picoScan100 with current firmware.
  • Access to the sensor web interface.

Both examples serve the host's local clock to the sensor subnet. Replace 192.168.0.0/24 with your sensor subnet.

chronyntpsec 
sudo apt update
sudo apt install chrony

Add these lines to /etc/chrony/chrony.conf:

# Serve the local system clock when no upstream server is reachable
local stratum 10
# Allow queries from the sensor subnet
allow 192.168.0.0/24

sudo systemctl restart chrony

sudo apt update
sudo apt install ntpsec

Add these lines to /etc/ntpsec/ntp.conf:

# Serve the local system clock when no upstream server is reachable
tos orphan 10
# Allow queries from the sensor subnet
restrict 192.168.0.0 mask 255.255.255.0 nomodify notrap

sudo systemctl restart ntpsec

On the picoScan100, open the sensor web interface (for example, http://192.168.0.1/) and navigate to Configuration → Basic Settings → Time Synchronization (NTP). Choose the time zone and update rate, enter the Ubuntu server's IP address (for example, 192.168.0.11), and save. Initial synchronization depends on the selected update rate; check its status in the sensor web interface.

Date and system time tile in SOPASair.

docs.title: Verify and Troubleshoot NTP
docs.text:
Check the server service and its clock, query it locally, inspect NTP traffic, and allow UDP port 123 through UFW if that firewall is enabled:

chronyntpsec 
systemctl status chrony
chronyc tracking
sudo chronyc clients

systemctl status ntpsec
ntpq -p

For both servers, watch the NTP traffic and open UDP port 123 in UFW if needed:

sudo tcpdump -i any udp port 123 -v
sudo ufw allow 123/udp

The sensor cannot act as an NTP server.

docs.title: Configure NTP Through REST or CoLa
docs.text:
Through REST, set TSCRole to 1 for NTP client mode and TSCTCSrvAddr to the server address. TSCRole accepts 0 (no time synchronization), 1 (NTP client), and 3 (PTP slave); other values are rejected with header.status 9 (Illegal Value). LSPdatetime reads the current sensor time and LSPsetdatetime sets it manually.

Ensure that the sensor can reach the selected NTP server through the configured network and firewall. For device-specific parameters and telegrams, see the LRS4000 REST / CoLa, multiScan100 REST / CoLa, multiScan200 REST / CoLa, and picoScan100 REST / CoLa references.

docs.title: PTP Time Synchronization
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

For high-precision synchronization on a local network, use the Precision Time Protocol (PTP) with the sensor and grandmaster settings below.

Date and system time settings with PTP selected.

docs.title: Sensor Settings
docs.text:
The sensor uses the following fixed IEEE 1588 PTPv2 settings, which cannot be changed:

Sensor Settings: parameter, fixed value, and description.

Parameter Value Description PTP profile IEEE 1588 PTPv2 E2E End-to-End delay mechanism Step mode Auto-detected Software PTP: one-step; hardware PTP: two-step Clock mode Ordinary clock Receives time synchronization from a master clock clockClass 255 Slave-only operation

docs.title: Master Configuration
docs.text:
Configure the PTP grandmaster with settings compatible with the sensor:

Master Configuration: parameter, required value, and description.

Parameter Required value Description PTP profile IEEE 1588 PTPv2 E2E End-to-End delay mechanism Transport protocol UDPv4 UDP over IPv4 logAnnounceInterval 1 (2 seconds) Interval between announce messages logSyncInterval 0 (1 second) Interval between synchronization messages announceReceiptTimeout 3 Timeout after three missing announce intervals logMinDelayReqInterval 0 (1 second) Minimum interval between Delay_Req messages Domain number 0 Must match the LiDAR's domain

Enable PTP in the sensor time-synchronization settings, or set TSCRole to 3 through the REST API, then connect it to this compatible PTP grandmaster. All participating devices must use the same domain, and network infrastructure must forward PTP traffic correctly.

With native ROS 2 on multiScan200 and picoScan100, the device publishes its hardware PTP timestamp in each message header. See Native ROS 2 for the available topics.

picoScan100 example: Enable PTP on the sensor after configuring a compatible grandmaster as described above. Menu labels may differ with firmware.

docs.title: UDP Unicast / Multicast
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 picoScan100

Measurement data can be sent over UDP unicast, UDP multicast, or TCP. UDP output is available on multiScan100 and picoScan100. multiScan200 and LRS4000 send Compact data over TCP.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Transport comparison: transport, communication, connection, delivery, and overhead.

Transport Communication Connection Delivery guarantee Overhead Best for UDP unicast One-to-one Connectionless None Low Low-latency data to one host UDP multicast One-to-many Connectionless None Low; efficient for multiple receivers The same data to several hosts TCP One-to-one Connection-oriented Reliable, ordered, error-checked Higher Data integrity; PLCs

For the formats and ports per device, see Compact Format: Transport.

docs.title: UDP/IP Unicast (Single Cast)
docs.text: In the data output settings, select Compact as the Format and set Measurement data output IP address to the receiver's IP address.

docs.title: UDP/IP Multicast
docs.text:
In the data output settings, select Compact as the Format and set Measurement data output IP address to a multicast address in the range 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255. The sensor sends each packet once for the whole group, reducing network load.

Every receiver joins the multicast group and listens on the configured UDP port. Make sure that switches and routers forward multicast traffic, and use IGMP snooping when several receivers are connected.

picoScan100 example: Receive Compact measurement data over UDP multicast after selecting a multicast destination and preparing the receiving hosts.

docs.title: TCP/IP
docs.text: Use TCP when data integrity and order take priority over latency. The TCP formats and ports per device are listed in Compact Format: Transport; on the picoScan100, TCP output uses LMDscandata.

docs.title: User Levels
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

User levels control who can change the sensor configuration. Reading live data and status does not require a login, but configuration changes, methods, and protected API requests do.

User Levels: user level and factory state for all supported devices.

User level Factory state Service Enabled Maintenance Disabled Authorized Client Disabled

Only Service is enabled in the factory state on all supported devices. A Service-level user must enable the other levels before they can be selected. Activate only the levels required by the deployment, then assign and protect their passwords before handing the system over.

docs.title: Log In
docs.text:
Select an enabled user level in SOPASair and authenticate with its configured password. For the first connection and commissioning sequence, see Getting Started.

picoScan100 example: Log in to SOPASair before enabling or changing user levels. Use your deployment credentials; do not retain default passwords.

docs.title: Enabling a User Level
docs.text:
Log in to SOPASair with the Service user level, open the user-level management settings, enable the required level, and set its password. Save the configuration permanently with Write EEPROM so the setting persists after a power cycle.

Access this tile in SOPASair via Diagnostic → Cybersecurity.

picoScan100 example: Enable the user levels needed for protected interfaces, then save the configuration and set secure passwords as described above.

REST API clients enable or disable REST user levels with EnableUserLevel. In the challenge-response header.user field, write the levels as Service, Maintenance, and AuthorizedClient. CoLa A/B clients use EnableLegacyUserLevel for their respective user levels. Authenticate these changes as Service with challenge-response.

For device-specific commands, see the multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100 REST API references; CoLa user-level telegrams are listed for multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100.

docs.title: picoScan100 CoLa A/B Access
docs.text:
On picoScan100, Maintenance and Authorized Client are disabled by default to enforce authorization. A Service-level user can enable them in the GUI or over CoLa A/B. In the GUI, log in as Service and enable the required levels in the user-level settings. Over CoLa, first log in as Service, then use EnableLegacyUserLevel with level 2 for Maintenance or 3 for Authorized Client and value 1 to enable it. See the picoScan100 CoLa telegram listing for the command structure. After enabling the required levels, run sMN Run to apply the change. The default passwords are documented in the operating instructions of your device. Do not pass them on, and change them during commissioning.

When upgrading from firmware earlier than V2.1.0 to V2.1.0, previously enabled user levels remain enabled. A factory reset restores the defaults: Service enabled, Maintenance and Authorized Client disabled.

A driver configured to log in as a disabled Maintenance or Authorized Client user may receive SetAccessMode 0 (login rejected); a subsequent protected write may return sFA A (write not permitted, for example because login is missing). Enable the user level in the device or configure the client to use Service. For example, sick_scan_xd supports selecting the user level with its user_level parameter from version V3.7 (3 for Client or 4 for Service); consult its picoScan launch configuration for the supported settings.

docs.title: Resetting the Password
docs.text:
1. Open the device's web interface and select Log In → Password forgotten?.
  2. Email the device key, serial number, and part number to your SICK sales company or service partner to obtain a one-time reset code.
  3. Click Next to open the code-entry window. You may close it with x and reopen it later via Settings → Password forgotten? without interrupting the reset. Selecting Cancel or repeatedly entering an incorrect code terminates the process and invalidates the code; restart the reset process.
  4. Enter the code and click Reset. The password returns to its default; device parameters remain unchanged.

docs.title: Simulation
docs.text:
Choose a virtual web interface to explore device configuration, or a robotics simulator to test sensor models in a scene.

  • Virtual Sensor Lab: run virtual sensor web interfaces in your browser.
  • NVIDIA Isaac Sim: use SICK LiDAR models in simulated environments.

docs.title: NVIDIA Isaac Sim
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 picoScan100

NVIDIA Isaac Sim provides simulation environments for robotics, industrial automation, and autonomous systems. SICK LiDAR models let you test applications and algorithms before physical hardware is available.

SICK models are available for picoScan150, picoScan120, multiScan136, multiScan165, and LRS4581R. multiScan200 models are coming soon. Find them on the applicable SICK product page under Downloads > Software or in NVIDIA Omniverse's sensor library. Configure the mounting position, orientation, field of view, scan frequency, detection range, and environment to match the deployment.

Search for the product family on sick.com:

  • LRS4000
  • multiScan100
  • picoScan100

Preview of a simulated multiScan270 (multiScan200, coming soon) scanning railway tracks in NVIDIA Omniverse, with the point cloud overlaid on the scene.

For more details on Isaac Sim, see:

  • What is Isaac Sim
  • Getting Started Tutorials

docs.title: Virtual Sensor Lab
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The cloud-based SICK Virtual Sensor Lab runs a live virtual sensor in your browser, so you can explore its web UI without hardware.

Open it at devices.cloud.sick.com.

  • Explore every menu of the web UI and change settings, for example the data output or field-evaluation zones.
  • Prepare a configuration offline, export it, and import it into a real device later. Configuration files from real devices can also be loaded and viewed.
  • It does not replace commissioning or a function test on the real device. .sopas files cannot be imported or exported.

SICK Virtual Sensor Lab product selection interface.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Start here when a sensor does not connect, does not send data, or reports an error.

  • Common Issues: symptom and check tables for connection, configuration, and measurement data.
  • Diagnostics: create a diagnostic file on the device and send it to SICK for analysis.
  • Error Codes: interpret reported errors and recommended actions.

docs.title: Get Support
docs.text: Create a diagnostic file in SOPASair (Diagnostics → Overview → Diagnostic file) and send it to SICK with a description of the problem. See Diagnostics and Contact.

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Quick fixes for the problems you are most likely to encounter during commissioning and integration. Each row links to the page with the details. Available settings, protocols, and menu paths vary by device family and firmware. Use the relevant device guide and release notes to confirm support.

docs.title: Connection
docs.text:
Connection: symptom and check.

Symptom Check Sensor not reachable / ping fails Computer and sensor in the same subnet; power and Ethernet connected (Getting Started) IP address unknown Device Discovery: SOPAS ET search, or ARP when device search is disabled Lost connection after an IP change Move the computer to the new subnet, or use device search to find the sensor IP change through device search is rejected The default IP change policy allows it only within 60 s after boot; reboot or log in (IP Address Assignment) Web UI does not load Open http://<ip>/ in Chrome, Edge, or Firefox; clear the cache; check that the web server is not disabled (Cybersecurity) HTTPS refuses connections after a certificate upload Read httpsStatus over HTTP on port 80, fix the certificate, and upload it again (HTTPS & Certificates)

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration: symptom and check.

Symptom Check Cannot change settings in the web UI Log in with an enabled user level; without login, the UI is read-only REST response has header.status 4 (Access Denied) The HTTP status is always 200; check header.status. Fetch a new challenge for every POST, check the password and that the user level is enabled, and wait 30 s after five failed logins (REST Interface) REST file transfer returns 403 Send a valid X-Session-Token header (Backup & Restore) Settings lost after power cycle Persist with WriteEeprom or Save permanently (REST Interface) CoLa sFA error response Look up the CoLa error code Web UI shows an error ID Look up the ID in the Error Codes list Need to restore factory settings How to perform a factory reset Firmware update stuck or fails Do not power-cycle while UpdateState is 1; allow 2-5 minutes for flash and reboot; on 3 (Error), check for the correct .spk.signed package (Firmware Update)

docs.title: Measurement Data
docs.text:
Measurement Data: symptom and check.

Symptom Check No UDP data arrives Data output enabled and destination IP/port set to your computer; Windows network profile set to Private; firewall allows the UDP port (Compact Format) No TCP data on LRS4000 or multiScan200 The sensor sends Compact over TCP only while a client is connected; connect to port 2115 (Compact Format) LMDscandata returns only zeros The output format is not set to LMDscandata; sRN LMDscandata then answers without an error (LMDscandata Format) Scan view empty Measurement is active and data output is enabled in the device's web interface CRC errors in your parser Compact: CRC32 over the whole frame; MSGPACK: CRC32 over the MSGPACK buffer only (MSGPACK Format) Fewer points than expected Filters and scan range reduce or zero out points No ROS 2 topics visible on a device with Native ROS 2 support Cyclone DDS configured with the host interface IP; matching domain ID (Native ROS 2) WebSocket closes with error 1002 on a device with WebSocket support Check the negotiated extensions and firmware; use a client compatible with the negotiated mode (WebSocket Events) Reduced range or warnings Check contamination indication and clean the optics cover

If the problem persists, create a diagnostic file and contact SICK.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

If you cannot solve a problem with the Troubleshooting tables or the Error Codes, create a diagnostic file on the device. The file collects diagnostic data of the device in one ZIP archive. SICK uses it to analyze the problem.

docs.title: SOPASair Diagnostics
docs.text:
Open the web interface of the device and go to Diagnostics → Overview. The page shows the current device status, the message log, and the Diagnostic file tile.

SOPASair Diagnostics → Overview on a picoScan100: status, messages, and the Diagnostic file tile with Create file and Download.

docs.title: Create and Send a Diagnostic File
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the problem, or create the file soon after it occurs.
  2. Log in with the Service user level or higher.
  3. In the Diagnostic file tile, click Create file. A new file overwrites the previous one, and the previous file can no longer be downloaded.
  4. Click Download and save the ZIP file on your computer.
  5. Send the file to SICK through your local SICK contact for analysis. Add a short description of the problem, the part number, the serial number, and the firmware version. See Contact for the contact options.

You can also create the file over the REST API with DoDiagnosisDump. See the REST API | OpenAPI page of your device for the available diagnostic endpoints.

The diagnostic file may contain information about your installation. Do not post it in public forums.

docs.title: More Information
docs.text: The operating instructions of your device describe the diagnostic functions, the status LEDs, and the messages in more detail. Download them from the Downloads tab of the product page on sick.com, or open the downloads section of your device guide: LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, or picoScan100.

docs.title: Error Codes
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The device reports problems with a customer error ID. The web interface shows the ID together with a short description and a recommended action. The list below omits codes for functions that these devices do not have, such as CAN, cameras, and SensorApps. Not every remaining code applies to every device.

Error Codes: error ID, description, and action.

Error ID Description and action 110 The device is defective. Return the device after consulting your SICK contact. 120 Switch off the device and restart it after 20 seconds. If the error occurs repeatedly, contact your SICK contact. 130 The firmware update failed. Install the firmware again after 2 minutes. If that does not work, install the last working firmware. 140 The system plug is defective. Replace the system plug. 205 The firmware update failed. The device uses the last active firmware. Restart the firmware update after 2 minutes. 210 The device is not ready for operation. Wait, and restart the device if the error persists. 211 Object evaluation is not active in interlaced mode. Deactivate interlaced mode to use object evaluation. 215 Measurement data is missing. 220 The device temperature is not OK. Check the ambient operating temperature. If necessary, use a heater or ensure sufficient cooling. 223 The device temperature is too low. Check the ambient operating temperature. If necessary, use a heater. 225 The device temperature is too high. Check the ambient operating temperature. If necessary, ensure sufficient cooling. 227 The motor speed is not OK. Check the device for external mechanical influences. 228 Shock or vibration exceeds the specification. 229 Dazzling detected. 230 The device is contaminated and not ready for operation. Clean the optics cover. 235 The device is not ready for operation. Wait. If the error persists, contact your SICK contact. 237 The device is not ready for operation. A parameterization problem was detected. Restart the device. If that does not help, contact your SICK contact. 239 Internal communication error detected. Switch off the device and restart it after 20 seconds. 240 The device and the system plug are not connected correctly. Check the connection and clean it if necessary. If the error occurs repeatedly, contact your SICK contact. 241 New system plug detected. The available inputs and outputs may have changed. Check the input and output configuration and all functions that use inputs and outputs. 250 The inertial measurement unit (IMU) is faulty. Restart the device. If that does not help, return the device after consulting your SICK contact. 505 Fallback mode is active. Disconnect the device from the power supply for about 20 seconds and restart it. 510 The device is temporarily not receiving measurement data. 511 The rotation speed deviates from the target value but is within the tolerated range: (f ≥ 15 Hz and f < 19 Hz) or (f > 21 Hz and f ≤ 25 Hz). Measurement data is still output. 520 The heater cannot be switched on. Check the power supply and the cable length and cross-section. 523 The temperature is close to the lower temperature limit. 525 The temperature is close to the upper temperature limit. 530 The device is contaminated and has limited functionality. Clean the optics cover. 540 Check the communication connection and settings. 543 A data packet could not be sent because a previous packet was not transmitted completely. Possible causes are a slow network connection or delayed data processing on the receiver side. Receive the data in a separate thread and use sufficiently large buffers. 545 Communication with the external time server (PTP, NTP) is not possible. Check the network settings. 547 The synchronization signal is missing. Check the wiring and the settings of the sync primary. 550 No connection to the internal additional sensors. Wait, and restart the device if necessary. 551 Measurement data of the inertial measurement unit (IMU) is missing. 560 I/O problem detected. Check the wiring and the configuration of the inputs and outputs. 562 The system plug memory could not be read. The system plug is defective or contains no data. Save the parameter set permanently on the system plug. If the error persists, check how the system plug is mounted on the device and replace the system plug if necessary. 563 The system plug memory could not be written. Check how the system plug is mounted on the device. 564 The input voltage is too high. Check whether the device is damaged. 565 The input voltage is too low. Inputs and outputs no longer work. 570 Parameterization problem detected. Check the configured parameters. 580 The HTTPS settings are faulty. Check the certificate on the Cybersecurity page. 581 Error while processing the certificate. Restart the device. If that does not help, return the device after consulting your SICK contact. 610 Too many fields are active at the same time. Reduce the number of simultaneously active fields or adjust the field size. 709 System plug without Gigabit Ethernet detected. This can cause loss of measurement data. Use a Gigabit Ethernet system plug. 710 Customer-specific setting. 715 The laser is switched off automatically by a customer-specific setting. 720 The device parameters differ from those on the cloning plug. The parameters from the cloning plug are applied. 810 Service mode. 905 The application is not loaded or not activated. Check the firmware. 907 The operation could not be completed because licenses are missing. Activate the required licenses and repeat the operation. 910 Too many functions are active at the same time. Deactivate functions that are not needed. 911 Object tracking is overloaded, for example because the device is moving. Switch off the object tracking function. 916 The output data is invalid. Restart the device. 918 Application error: See Diagnostics in the user interface of the application or the product documentation. 935 One of the inputs used is not available or is used more than once. Check the functions that use ports as inputs. 940 The device is not ready for operation. Restart the device. If the error still occurs, reset the device to factory settings or change the parameterization. 990 Application error: The parameters are invalid. Check the configured parameters. If necessary, reset to factory settings. 992 The configuration was not applied because of an internal error. The device uses the last saved configuration. Configure the device again. If that does not work, restart the device.

docs.title: Choose a Visualization Tool
docs.text:
Choose a tool based on whether you need to configure a live sensor, manage devices and firmware, locate a device, or inspect point-cloud files.

  • SOPASair: configure and commission a connected sensor in its browser-based interface, including interactive workflows such as field teach-in and firmware update. Start here.
  • ROS 2 rviz: view live ROS 2 topics and point clouds to check data flow, frame alignment, and scan coverage; requires a running ROS 2 setup.
  • CloudCompare: inspect and process saved 3D point clouds, including compatible PCD files; for offline work, not live sensor configuration.
  • Sentio Creator: discover and commission SICK devices and find matching firmware packages; requires installing the SICK software.
  • SOPAS ET: use the legacy engineering tool across all device families for network discovery and CoLa commands; use SOPASair for supported device setup.

docs.title: CloudCompare
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

CloudCompare is a free, open-source 3D point-cloud viewer and processing tool. You can use it to visualize .pcd files produced by 3D scan recording or by the sick_perception_sdk, without writing any viewer code yourself.

LiDAR point cloud displayed in CloudCompare 2.13.2.

  1. Open the .pcd file with File → Open.
  2. If the file contains intensity, select the cloud and set Colors to Scalar field with intensity as the active field in the Properties panel.
  3. Use the Point picking tool to measure the distance between two points.

docs.title: ROS 2 rviz
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Use rviz2 to inspect SICK LiDAR point clouds, laser scans, and coordinate frames from native ROS 2 or sick_scan_xd.

  1. Configure the sensor for ROS 2 output as described in ROS Integration.
  2. Start the ROS 2 middleware and sensor publisher. For native ROS 2, use Cyclone DDS; for sick_scan_xd, start the driver on the host.
  3. Confirm that ROS 2 can see the sensor topics:
ros2 topic list

For native ROS 2, /cloud/all_points is the combined point cloud. A sick_scan_xd launch can use different topic names; select the sensor_msgs/msg/PointCloud2 or sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan topic shown by ros2 topic list. 4. Launch rviz2 in the same sourced ROS 2 environment:

rviz2
  1. In the left panel, add a display such as:
  2. PointCloud2 for a dense 3D point cloud,
  3. LaserScan for 2D planar output,
  4. TF to verify coordinate frames,
  5. Axes to confirm sensor orientation.
  6. Select the published topic, set the fixed frame, and check the sensor data against the expected field of view.

Set Reliability Policy to match the publisher when rviz2 reports an incompatible QoS profile. Check that data arrives on the topic:

ros2 topic info --verbose /cloud/all_points
ros2 topic echo --once /cloud/all_points

Replace the topic for a sick_scan_xd launch. If data arrives but rviz2 shows a No transform error, set Fixed Frame to the message's header.frame_id, or publish the required static transform.

docs.title: Sentio Creator
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Sentio Creator is a SICK software tool, published on sick.com, used to configure and commission supported SICK devices. Alongside the device's product page, it is also a source for firmware update packages. Use it to obtain the correct package for your device variant before running a firmware update.

Sentio Creator software interface displaying device list and extensions manager.

docs.title: SOPAS ET
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

SOPAS ET is a legacy SICK engineering tool that works with all device families in this guide. Use SOPASair for supported device setup and configuration workflows.

SOPAS Engineering Tool interface with device search and project view.

SOPAS ET can still be useful for discovering sensors on the local network. Use its network search to locate a device when its IP address is unknown, then continue commissioning in SOPASair or through the REST API.

SOPAS ET also includes the SOPAS ET Terminal feature, which can send CoLa A and CoLa B commands to sensors over TCP.

SICK knowledge base video: search for the device with SOPAS ET.

docs.title: SOPASair
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

SOPASair is the sensor's built-in web UI, served directly from the device at http://192.168.0.1/ with factory settings. There is nothing to install: point a browser at the sensor. Use it to:

  • configure the settings available on the selected device,
  • draw or teach in field-evaluation zones where the device supports those functions,
  • update firmware through the web UI where supported, or use the documented REST sequence,
  • create a diagnostic file if the device provides that option.

Screen-by-screen walkthroughs are available for the LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100. Available menus and functions vary by product family, variant, and firmware. For standard IP address settings, see Getting Started.

For measurement recordings, see the SOPASair Data recorder if that function is available on your device.

Live capture from a picoScan100's SOPASair web interface.
